u1.intro: A periodic table and the AP Chemistry equations sheet are allowed, and a calculator may be used throughout.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-4 refer to the following.

Lithium from different sources can have different isotopic compositions. A chemist records the mass spectrum of two samples of pure lithium metal. Every peak is produced by singly charged Li⁺ ions, and the peak heights are given relative to the tallest peak in each spectrum.
Sample · height at m/z 6 · height at m/z 7
A (from a lithium mineral) · 8.2 · 100
B (from a commercial supplier) · 3.0 · 100
Isotopic masses: ⁶Li 6.015 amu, ⁷Li 7.016 amu. The periodic table lists lithium as 6.94 g/mol. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.q:
Which of the following is closest to the average atomic mass of lithium in sample B?
(A) 6.52 amu
(B) 6.94 amu
(C) 6.99 amu
(D) 7.20 amu
parts.a: (C). Heights scaled to the tallest peak must first be turned into fractions of their total, 3.0 + 100 = 103.0: ⁶Li is 3.0/103.0 = 0.0291 and ⁷Li is 100/103.0 = 0.9709 of the atoms. The weighted average is 0.0291(6.015) + 0.9709(7.016) = 6.99 amu. (A) is the plain mean of 6.015 and 7.016, which ignores how few atoms are ⁶Li. (B) is the average for sample A (0.0758 ⁶Li gives 6.940 amu), the periodic-table value, not the value for B. (D) divides the weighted sum 3.0(6.015) + 100(7.016) by 100 instead of by 103.0, treating heights relative to the tallest peak as if they were percentages; an average above the heavier isotope's mass is impossible.
parts.n: 1.2.A.2 (topic 1.2), skill 5.D. Thinking: convert relative peak heights to fractional abundances, then weight each isotopic mass. Trap: (D), dividing by 100 when the heights do not add to 100.

parts.q:
A chemist uses the periodic-table value, 6.94 g/mol, to calculate the number of moles of lithium atoms in a 1.000 g piece of sample B. How does the calculated value compare with the true value?
(A) It is slightly too high, because the atoms in B are heavier on average than 6.94 g/mol assumes, so 1.000 g of B holds fewer atoms than calculated.
(B) It is slightly too low, because the atoms in B are heavier on average than 6.94 g/mol assumes, so 1.000 g of B holds more atoms than calculated.
(C) It is exactly right, because isotopes of an element have identical chemical properties, so every sample of the element has the same molar mass.
(D) It is slightly too low, because B contains fewer ⁶Li atoms than sample A, and the lighter atoms are the ones that a mass measurement counts.
parts.a: (A). Sample B's average atomic mass is 6.99 amu, so its molar mass is 6.99 g/mol. The true amount is 1.000 g ÷ 6.987 g/mol = 0.1431 mol, but the chemist calculates 1.000 g ÷ 6.94 g/mol = 0.1441 mol, about 0.7% too high: dividing a mass by a molar mass that is too small overcounts the particles. (B) has the right premise but inverts n = m/M: heavier particles mean fewer of them in a fixed mass, not more. (C) confuses chemical behavior, which isotopes share, with mass, which they do not; the molar mass depends on the isotope mixture. (D) invents a rule: a balance weighs every atom in the piece, light and heavy alike.
parts.n: 1.1.A.3 and 1.2.A.2 (topic 1.1), skill 5.C. Thinking: in n = m/M, a molar mass that is too small makes n too large. Trap: (B), which reasons that heavier atoms mean more atoms per gram.

parts.q:
A student argues that sample B cannot be pure lithium: its average atomic mass differs from 6.94 amu, so it must contain an impurity heavier than lithium. Which of the following best evaluates the argument?
(A) The argument is sound, because the average atomic mass of an element is a fixed constant, so any sample that differs from 6.94 amu must contain another element.
(B) The argument is sound, because the m/z 7 peak of sample B is taller than that of sample A, which shows extra heavy particles in sample B.
(C) The argument is flawed, because a heavier impurity would have lowered the average atomic mass of sample B below that of sample A.
(D) The argument is flawed, because B's spectrum shows peaks only at m/z 6 and 7; its higher average comes from a smaller share of ⁶Li, not from another element.
parts.a: (D). An impurity heavier than lithium would produce peaks at its own m/z values, and B's spectrum has only the two lithium peaks. What differs is their ratio: ⁶Li is 7.6% of the atoms in A but only 2.9% in B, so B's weighted average (6.99 amu) is closer to 7.016. (A) treats the tabulated average as a constant of nature; it is an average over typical sources, and isotopic composition varies with source. (B) misreads the data: both spectra are scaled so the m/z 7 peak is 100, so the m/z 7 peaks are the same height by construction; it is the m/z 6 peak that differs. (C) reaches the right verdict for a false reason: a heavier impurity would raise the average, not lower it.
parts.n: 1.2.A.1 and 1.2.A.2 (topic 1.2), skill 6.B. Thinking: a mass spectrum shows which particles are present; a shift in the average with no new peaks means a new isotope ratio, not a new element. Trap: (A), treating 6.94 amu as a fixed constant.

parts.q:
The label falls off a third bottle of lithium, which is known to be either sample A or sample B. Which procedure would identify the sample?
(A) Measure the first ionization energy of the lithium; the sample richer in ⁷Li holds its outer electron more tightly.
(B) Burn the lithium in oxygen and determine the empirical formula of the oxide, which differs for the two samples.
(C) Record the mass spectrum and compare the height of the m/z 6 peak, relative to the m/z 7 peak, with 8.2 and 3.0.
(D) Burn 0.500 g of the lithium to Li₂O and weigh the oxide on a balance that reads to the nearest 0.01 g.
parts.a: (C). The two samples differ only in the ratio of their isotopes, and the mass spectrum measures that ratio directly: a relative m/z 6 height near 8.2 means sample A and one near 3.0 means sample B. (A) fails because isotopes have the same nuclear charge and the same electrons, so their ionization energies are essentially identical. (B) fails because both samples are lithium, and lithium forms Li₂O whatever its isotopes. (D) is a real difference that the balance cannot detect: 0.500 g of lithium gives 0.500 + 4.00/6.940 = 1.076 g of Li₂O for A and 0.500 + 4.00/6.987 = 1.073 g for B, a difference of 0.004 g, smaller than the balance's 0.01 g resolution.
parts.n: 1.2.A.1 (topic 1.2), skill 2.C. Thinking: choose a measurement that responds to the one property that differs, and check that its precision can resolve the difference. Trap: (D), which ignores the balance's resolution.

mc.stem:
Questions 5-8 refer to the following.

To find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide, a student heats a coiled strip of magnesium ribbon in a covered crucible, lifting the lid slightly from time to time to let air in, until the metal no longer glows. She cools the crucible and weighs it, then reheats, cools and reweighs it until the mass stops changing.
Measurement · mass (g)
Crucible and lid · 26.318
Crucible, lid and magnesium · 26.561
Crucible, lid and product (constant mass) · 26.714
Molar masses (g/mol): Mg 24.31, O 16.00, N 14.01.

parts.q:
Which of the following is the mole ratio of oxygen to magnesium in the product, as calculated from the student's data?
(A) 0.63
(B) 0.96
(C) 1.05
(D) 1.59
parts.a: (B). m(Mg) = 26.561 − 26.318 = 0.243 g, so n(Mg) = 0.243 ÷ 24.31 = 9.996 × 10⁻³ mol. The oxygen gained is 26.714 − 26.561 = 0.153 g, so n(O) = 0.153 ÷ 16.00 = 9.56 × 10⁻³ mol, and O : Mg = 9.56 × 10⁻³ ÷ 9.996 × 10⁻³ = 0.96. (A) is the mass ratio, 0.153 g ÷ 0.243 g, taken before either mass is converted to moles. (C) is the mole ratio inverted, Mg : O. (D) is the inverted mass ratio, 0.243 ÷ 0.153; an empirical formula compares numbers of atoms, not masses.
parts.n: 1.3.A.3 and 1.1.A.3 (topic 1.3), skill 5.F. Thinking: get each element's mass by difference, convert both to moles, then take the ratio in the order asked. Trap: (A), comparing masses instead of moles.

parts.q:
The accepted formula of magnesium oxide is MgO. Which of the following could account for the difference between the student's ratio and the ratio in MgO?
(A) The product took up water vapor from the air while it cooled on the bench before each of its weighings.
(B) Some of the white product escaped as smoke each time the lid was lifted to let air into the crucible.
(C) The balance read every mass 0.050 g too high, including the mass of the empty crucible and its lid.
(D) Soot from the burner flame collected on the outside of the crucible while the magnesium was burning.
parts.a: (B). The student's ratio, 0.96, is below the 1.00 of MgO, so the mass gained was too small for the magnesium used. Product that escapes as smoke carries off magnesium as well as oxygen, but the magnesium's mass was fixed by the earlier weighing; the loss shows up only as a smaller final mass, so the mass gain, all counted as oxygen, is too small and O : Mg comes out too low. (A) and (D) both add mass to the final weighing, which makes the calculated oxygen, and so the ratio, too high. (C) has no effect: every mass in the calculation is a difference between two weighings, and a constant 0.050 g offset cancels in each difference.
parts.n: 1.3.A.3 (topic 1.3), skill 6.G. Thinking: trace each error to the mass it changes, then to the ratio; a constant offset cancels in a difference. Trap: (A), which does change the result, but in the wrong direction.

parts.q:
Suppose that all of the magnesium reacted and that the product was a mixture of MgO and Mg₃N₂ only. Which of the following is closest to the percent of the product's mass that was Mg₃N₂?
(A) 1.7%
(B) 2.5%
(C) 8.8%
(D) 10.4%
parts.a: (C). Let x mol of Mg end up in MgO (40.31 g/mol) and y mol in Mg₃N₂ (100.95 g/mol, so 33.65 g per mole of Mg). Then x + y = 9.996 × 10⁻³ and 40.31x + 33.65y = 0.396 g, which give y = 1.04 × 10⁻³ mol. The nitride is y/3 = 3.47 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 100.95 g/mol = 0.0350 g, and 0.0350 ÷ 0.396 = 8.8% of the product. (D) is the fraction of the magnesium atoms that ended up in the nitride, 1.04 × 10⁻³ ÷ 9.996 × 10⁻³, not a mass percent of the product. (B) is the percent of the product that is nitrogen, 0.00972 g ÷ 0.396 g, which leaves out the magnesium in the nitride. (A) is the shortfall from the mass of pure MgO as a percent of it, (0.403 − 0.396) ÷ 0.403 = 1.7%, which is not the mass of the nitride.
parts.n: 1.4.A.1 and 1.4.A.2 (topic 1.4), skill 5.F. Thinking: a two-component mixture with a known total mass and a known total amount of one element gives two equations in two unknowns. Trap: (D), the percent of Mg atoms rather than the percent of the product's mass.

parts.q:
A classmate argues that the product is pure MgO, and that the whole difference between the student's ratio and the ratio in MgO comes from the limited precision of the balance, which reads to the nearest 0.001 g. Which of the following best evaluates the argument?
(A) It is supported, because the product was heated to constant mass, and a product at constant mass has reacted completely to form pure MgO.
(B) It is supported, because a measured mole ratio is rounded to a whole number, and the student's ratio rounds to the 1 : 1 ratio in MgO.
(C) It is not supported, because pure MgO has an O : Mg ratio of exactly 1, so any other measured ratio, however close, proves an impurity.
(D) It is not supported: the oxygen gained differs from the mass pure MgO needs by several times the smallest mass the balance can resolve.
parts.a: (D). Pure MgO would need 1 mol of O per mol of Mg: 9.996 × 10⁻³ mol × 16.00 g/mol = 0.160 g of oxygen, but the mass gained was 26.714 − 26.561 = 0.153 g. The gap, 0.007 g, is seven times the balance's 0.001 g reading; even if each mass found by difference were off by 0.001 g in the worst direction, the ratio would be at most (0.154 ÷ 16.00) ÷ (0.242 ÷ 24.31) = 0.97. So the shortfall is a real systematic error in the product or the procedure, not scatter in the weighings. (A) confuses a finished process with a pure product: constant mass shows that nothing more is changing, not that the product is MgO alone; Mg₃N₂ or unreacted Mg would also sit at constant mass. (B) uses rounding, which picks a formula but cannot show that a 4% shortfall is only scatter; the argument is about the size of the error. (C) reaches the right verdict with a rule that ignores measurement uncertainty: a ratio of 0.995 would lie within the balance's precision and would prove nothing.
parts.n: 1.3.A.2 and 1.4.A.1 (topic 1.3), skill 6.F. Thinking: compare the size of a discrepancy with the precision of the measurements before blaming it on scatter. Trap: (C), the right verdict from a rule that ignores measurement uncertainty.

mc.stem:
Questions 9-12 refer to the following.

The photoelectron spectra of three gaseous species, X, Y and Z, are recorded. The species are Cl⁻, Ar and K⁺, in some order, and each has 18 electrons. Every spectrum has five peaks, with relative heights 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 in order of decreasing binding energy. The table gives the approximate positions of the highest-energy and the lowest-energy peak in each spectrum.
Species · 1s peak (MJ/mol) · 3p peak (MJ/mol)
X · 309 · 1.52
Y · 347 · 3.05
Z · 273 · 0.35

parts.q:
Which of the following identifies species Y and gives the best reason?
(A) Y is K⁺, because its 19 protons attract the same 18 electrons, in the same subshells, as in X and Z.
(B) Y is Cl⁻, because its extra electron adds repulsion, and more repulsion makes each electron harder to remove.
(C) Y is Ar, because a neutral atom with a filled valence shell holds its electrons more tightly than an ion does.
(D) Y is K⁺, because a cation has lost its outer shell, so its electrons are in lower shells than those of X and Z.
parts.a: (A). The identical peak heights show that X, Y and Z have the same electrons in the same subshells, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶. What differs is the nuclear charge: 17 for Cl⁻, 18 for Ar and 19 for K⁺. With the same electrons shielding, the species with the most protons attracts every electron most strongly, so every one of its peaks sits at the highest binding energy; that is Y. (D) names the right species for a wrong reason: K⁺ has lost the 4s shell of a K atom, but compared with X and Z it has the same shells, as the matching peak heights show. (B) reverses the effect of repulsion: added repulsion makes electrons easier to remove, which is why Cl⁻ is Z, with the lowest peaks. (C) uses a slogan about filled shells, but all three species have the same filled shells, so that cannot set Ar apart.
parts.n: 1.6.A.1 and 1.5.A.4 (topic 1.6), skill 4.B. Thinking: equal peak heights mean equal configurations, so a uniform shift in peak positions must come from nuclear charge. Trap: (D), the right identity with a lost-shell reason that the spectra rule out.

parts.q:
A student claims that because X, Y and Z have the same electron configuration, the three species have the same radius. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) It is correct, because the radius of a species is set by its outermost occupied shell, and n = 3 is outermost in all three.
(B) It is incorrect: Y's higher binding energies show its electrons are held most strongly, so Y is smallest and Z largest.
(C) It is incorrect: Y's electrons have the highest binding energies because they are farthest out, so Y is the largest.
(D) It is incorrect: Z's low binding energies show its electrons are packed most tightly about its nucleus, so Z is smallest.
parts.a: (B). The same electrons are attracted by 19 protons in Y (K⁺), 18 in X (Ar) and 17 in Z (Cl⁻). A stronger Coulombic attraction pulls the electron cloud closer, which is what the higher binding energies show, so the radius order is Y < X < Z. (A) is half right: the outermost shell sets the approximate size, but within the same shell the nuclear charge still decides how tightly the cloud is drawn in. (C) reverses the link between energy and distance: electrons farther out are held less tightly and have lower binding energies. (D) makes the same reversal for Z: low binding energies mean weak attraction and a larger, looser cloud.
parts.n: 1.7.A.2 and 1.6.A.1 (topic 1.7), skill 6.C. Thinking: in an isoelectronic series the radius falls as the nuclear charge rises, and binding energy is the evidence. Trap: (A), stopping at 'same outer shell'.

parts.q:
The spectrum of Ca²⁺ also has five peaks, with heights 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6. Which of the following is the best estimate of the position of its 3p peak?
(A) About 0.59 MJ/mol, because the most weakly held electrons of calcium are its 4s electrons, and 0.59 MJ/mol removes one.
(B) About 3.05 MJ/mol, because Ca²⁺ has the same configuration as the species with the highest peaks, so it holds electrons equally.
(C) About 4.9 MJ/mol, because Ca²⁺ has more protons than X, Y or Z, attracting the same 18 electrons in the same subshells.
(D) About 6.1 MJ/mol, because doubling the ion's charge from 1+ to 2+ doubles the attraction on each of its electrons.
parts.a: (C). Ca²⁺ has 20 protons and the same 18 electrons, so the trend in the table continues. The 3p peak rises from 0.35 to 1.52 to 3.05 MJ/mol as the nuclear charge goes from 17 to 18 to 19, by 1.17 and then 1.53 MJ/mol; one more proton should raise it by a little more again, to roughly 4.9 MJ/mol. (A) describes a neutral Ca atom: Ca²⁺ has already lost both 4s electrons, so its outermost electrons are 3p. (B) is the claim that configuration alone sets binding energy, which the table itself refutes: X, Y and Z share a configuration but not peak positions. (D) ties the attraction to the ion's net charge; the table does not fit that idea (Ar has no net charge yet binds its 3p electrons at 1.52 MJ/mol), and one added proton raises the nuclear charge only from 19 to 20.
parts.n: 1.6.A.1 and 1.7.A.3 (topic 1.6), skill 4.A. Thinking: extend a data trend in nuclear charge to a new isoelectronic species. Trap: (B), which assumes the same configuration means the same binding energies.

parts.q:
Across the three species, the position of the 1s peak changes by about 74 MJ/mol, while the position of the 3p peak changes by only about 2.7 MJ/mol. Which of the following best explains why the 1s peak shifts so much more?
(A) The 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus and unshielded by inner electrons, so each added proton raises their attraction far more.
(B) There are six 3p electrons but only two 1s electrons, so the added proton's attraction is shared among more electrons in the 3p subshell.
(C) The six 3p electrons repel one another strongly, and their repulsion cancels most of the effect that each added proton has on them.
(D) The 1s peak is recorded first in each experiment, so the 1s electrons absorb more of each photon's energy than the 3p electrons do.
parts.a: (A). The three species differ only in nuclear charge (17, 18 and 19 protons), so both shifts come from added protons. Coulomb's law, F ∝ q₁q₂/r², says a change in the nuclear charge changes the attraction most for an electron at small r that feels the whole charge. The 1s electrons sit closest to the nucleus with nothing between them and it, so each added proton raises their binding energy by 36 to 38 MJ/mol. The 3p electrons are far out and screened by the ten n = 1 and n = 2 electrons, so the same proton changes their attraction only slightly. (B) treats attraction as a fixed amount divided among electrons; each electron feels the whole nucleus. (C) cannot explain a difference among X, Y and Z, since all three have the same six 3p electrons and so the same repulsion among them. (D) misreads PES: each peak's position is the energy needed to remove an electron from that subshell, not an amount absorbed in some order.
parts.n: 1.5.A.2 and 1.5.A.4 (topic 1.5), skill 4.A. Thinking: use distance and shielding in Coulomb's law to explain why the same change in nuclear charge affects inner and outer electrons differently. Trap: (C), a repulsion argument that does not vary across the three species.

mc.stem:
Questions 13-16 refer to the following.

A student adds 1 mL of an aqueous solution of a halogen to 2 mL of a 0.1 M aqueous potassium halide, then adds 1 mL of hexane, shakes the tube and lets the layers separate. Any halogen (X₂) present dissolves mostly in the hexane, the top layer, where Cl₂ is nearly colorless, Br₂ is orange and I₂ is violet. Halide ions stay in the colorless water layer.
Halogen added · hexane layer with KCl(aq) · with KBr(aq) · with KI(aq)
Cl₂(aq) · not tested · orange · violet
Br₂(aq) · orange · not tested · violet
I₂(aq) · violet · violet · not tested

parts.q:
Which of the following conclusions do the results support?
(A) Cl₂ took electrons from both Br⁻ and I⁻, Br₂ took electrons from I⁻ only, and I₂ took electrons from neither ion.
(B) Br₂ took electrons from both Cl⁻ and I⁻, because the hexane was colored in both of the tubes to which Br₂ was added.
(C) I₂ took electrons from both Cl⁻ and Br⁻, because the hexane turned violet in both of the tubes to which I₂ was added.
(D) Only Cl₂ reacted, because Br₂ and I₂ are colored before they react, so their rows show no change in any of the tubes.
parts.a: (A). A color that differs from the halogen added shows a new halogen formed. Cl₂ (nearly colorless) gave orange Br₂ with KBr and violet I₂ with KI, so Cl₂ + 2 Br⁻ → 2 Cl⁻ + Br₂ and Cl₂ + 2 I⁻ → 2 Cl⁻ + I₂. Br₂ gave violet with KI, so Br₂ took electrons from I⁻, but stayed orange with KCl, so nothing happened there. I₂ stayed violet in both tubes: no reaction. (B) and (C) read the color of the unreacted halogen, which was simply added to the tube, as evidence of a reaction. (D) overlooks that the Br₂ + KI tube turned violet, not orange, so the Br₂ was used up and I₂ formed.
parts.n: 1.8.A.1 (topic 1.8), skill 6.B. Thinking: separate 'the color I added' from 'a new color that formed' before drawing a conclusion. Trap: (B), reading the orange of unreacted Br₂ as a reaction with Cl⁻.

parts.q:
A student explains the results: 'Iodine is the least reactive halogen because an iodine atom has the most electrons, and they repel an incoming electron.' Which of the following best evaluates the explanation?
(A) It is complete, because the total number of electrons in an atom is what sets how strongly the atom attracts one more.
(B) It is wrong, because iodine has the most protons, so it should attract electrons most strongly; its low solubility explains the results.
(C) It is wrong, because iodine atoms are the heaviest, so they move most slowly and collide with the halide ions least often.
(D) It is incomplete: the electron iodine gains enters the n = 5 shell, farther out and more shielded, so it is held less strongly.
parts.a: (D). The electron an iodine atom gains goes into the n = 5 shell, which is farther from the nucleus than the n = 3 shell of chlorine, and 46 inner electrons shield it. Although iodine has more protons, the attraction the added electron feels is weaker, since Coulombic attraction falls with distance, so I₂ takes electrons least readily. The student's repulsion idea is part of shielding but leaves out distance, the main factor. (A) accepts the incomplete account. (B) counts protons without shielding and distance, then blames solubility, which the hexane test does not depend on. (C) offers a rate argument, but the data record whether a reaction happened, not how fast, and iodine did not react at all.
parts.n: 1.7.A.2 and 1.8.A.1 (topic 1.7), skill 6.D. Thinking: explain a reactivity trend with Coulomb's law, distance and shielding, not with a count of particles. Trap: (B), the 'more protons, stronger pull' argument that ignores shells.

parts.q:
Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the results?
(A) Br⁻ ions do not give up electrons to I₂ under these conditions.
(B) Cl₂ can take electrons from I⁻ ions under these conditions.
(C) Cl₂ reacts with Br⁻ faster than Br₂ reacts with I⁻ ions.
(D) I⁻ ions give up electrons more readily than Br⁻ ions do.
parts.a: (C). The table records only whether a new halogen formed, not how quickly, so it cannot compare the rates of two reactions. (A) is supported: I₂ with KBr stayed violet, so no Br₂ formed. (B) is supported: Cl₂ with KI turned violet. (D) is supported by the pair of tests between bromine and iodine: Br₂ took electrons from I⁻, but I₂ did not take electrons from Br⁻, so I⁻ loses electrons more readily.
parts.n: 1.8.A.1 (topic 1.8), skill 2.D. Thinking: match each statement with the observation it needs; these data show whether a reaction occurs, not its rate. Trap: (D), which is supported, but only by combining two observations.

parts.q:
Bromine is produced industrially from brines that contain Br⁻(aq) together with much more Cl⁻(aq). Based on the student's results, which of the following could be added to such a brine to produce Br₂?
(A) I₂, because iodine is the largest halogen, so it holds its own electrons most loosely and can release Br₂.
(B) Cl₂, because the results show Cl₂ takes electrons from Br⁻, and the Cl⁻ it forms is already in the brine.
(C) KI, because I⁻ ions give up their electrons readily, so they can supply the electrons that turn Br⁻ into Br₂.
(D) KCl, because Cl⁻ ions are more reactive than Br⁻ ions, so adding more of them pushes the Br⁻ out as Br₂.
parts.a: (B). Forming Br₂ from Br⁻ means removing electrons from Br⁻ (2 Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2 e⁻), so the reagent must take electrons from Br⁻. The results show Cl₂ does this: Cl₂ + 2 Br⁻ → 2 Cl⁻ + Br₂, and the Cl⁻ it leaves behind is already the main ion in the brine. (A) contradicts the data: I₂ with KBr stayed violet, so I₂ cannot oxidize Br⁻. (C) has the direction of electron flow backward: supplying electrons to Br⁻ cannot make Br₂. (D) treats Cl⁻ ions as reactive like Cl₂; halide ions, with filled valence shells, do not take electrons, and the brine is already full of Cl⁻.
parts.n: 1.8.A.1 and 1.8.A.2 (topic 1.8), skill 4.A. Thinking: turn a ranking from a test-tube experiment into a choice of reagent for a new context. Trap: (C), which confuses giving electrons with taking them.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-19 refer to the following.

A garden-supply company sells a fertilizer labeled 'urea, CO(NH₂)₂'. A laboratory finds that a 2.500 g sample of it contains 1.050 g of nitrogen, which is 42.0% N by mass. Two hypotheses are proposed.
H1: the fertilizer is urea mixed with sand, SiO₂.
H2: the fertilizer is urea mixed with ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Substance · molar mass (g/mol) · mass percent N · mass percent C
Urea, CO(NH₂)₂ · 60.06 · 46.65 · 20.00
Ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄ · 132.15 · 21.20 · 0
Sand, SiO₂ · 60.08 · 0 · 0

parts.q:
If H1 is correct, which of the following is closest to the mass percent of urea in the fertilizer?
(A) 42.0%
(B) 90.0%
(C) 95.4%
(D) 81.7%
parts.a: (B). Under H1 all of the nitrogen comes from urea, and urea is 46.65% N, so the fraction of urea in the sample is 42.0 ÷ 46.65 = 0.900, or 90.0% (2.251 g of urea in the 2.500 g sample). (A) reads the percent nitrogen as the percent urea, as if urea were all nitrogen. (C) subtracts the percentages, 100 − (46.65 − 42.0); a mixture's composition is a weighted average, not a difference. (D) is the answer under H2, where the ammonium sulfate supplies some of the nitrogen; it does not apply when the impurity is sand.
parts.n: 1.4.A.2 (topic 1.4), skill 5.F. Thinking: when only one component contains the element, the element's mass percent scales the component's mass percent. Trap: (A), treating percent N as percent urea.

parts.q:
A student claims that the nitrogen analysis proves the fertilizer is at least 90% urea, whichever hypothesis is correct. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) It is correct, because 42.0% ÷ 46.65% = 90.0% whatever the impurity is, since the analysis detects only the nitrogen in urea.
(B) It is correct, because an impurity that contains nitrogen adds to the urea's nitrogen, so more of the sample must be urea.
(C) It cannot be judged, because a nitrogen analysis says nothing at all about the amount of urea unless the sample is pure.
(D) It is incorrect: 90.0% is the most urea the sample can hold, because nitrogen in the impurity means less urea is needed.
parts.a: (D). If the impurity has no nitrogen, all 42.0% N comes from urea and the sample is 90.0% urea. If the impurity contains nitrogen, as in H2, some of the 42.0% comes from it, so less urea is needed: 81.7% for ammonium sulfate. 90.0% is therefore an upper limit, not a lower one. (A) assumes the analysis tells urea nitrogen from other nitrogen; it measures all of it. (B) reverses the reasoning: nitrogen from the impurity replaces urea nitrogen, lowering the urea needed. (C) goes too far: without knowing the impurity, the analysis still sets a limit on the urea content.
parts.n: 1.4.A.2 (topic 1.4), skill 6.D. Thinking: test the claim against each hypothesis; a result that holds only when the impurity has no nitrogen gives a bound, not a value. Trap: (B), which gets the direction of the effect backward.

parts.q:
Which of the following additional results would support H2 rather than H1?
(A) The fertilizer is 20.0% carbon by mass.
(B) The fertilizer is 18.0% carbon by mass.
(C) The fertilizer is 16.3% carbon by mass.
(D) A second sample is also 42.0% nitrogen.
parts.a: (C). Only urea contains carbon, so percent C = (fraction urea) × 20.00%. Under H1 the sample is 90.0% urea, giving 0.900 × 20.00 = 18.0% C. Under H2 the fraction x of urea satisfies 46.65x + 21.20(1 − x) = 42.0, so x = 20.8 ÷ 25.45 = 0.817 and the sample is 0.817 × 20.00 = 16.3% C. (B) is the result H1 predicts, so it would support H1 instead. (A) is the carbon content of pure urea, which neither hypothesis predicts, and a pure sample would be 46.65% N. (D) repeats the original measurement, which both hypotheses were built to fit, so it cannot tell them apart.
parts.n: 1.4.A.2 (topic 1.4), skill 2.C. Thinking: work out what each hypothesis predicts for a new measurement and pick the result only one of them predicts. Trap: (B), the value H1 predicts.

parts.q:
A tablet containing 1.50 g of calcium carbonate supplies 600 mg of calcium. A patient who switches to calcium citrate, Ca₃(C₆H₅O₇)₂ (molar mass 498.4 g/mol), wants the same 600 mg of calcium. What mass of calcium citrate supplies it? (Ca = 40.08 g/mol)
(A) 2.49 g
(B) 1.50 g
(C) 7.46 g
(D) 0.145 g
parts.a: (A). 0.600 g Ca ÷ 40.08 g/mol = 1.497 × 10⁻² mol Ca. Each formula unit of the citrate holds 3 Ca, so 1.497 × 10⁻² ÷ 3 = 4.99 × 10⁻³ mol of citrate, and 4.99 × 10⁻³ mol × 498.4 g/mol = 2.49 g. (B) assumes that equal masses of the two compounds supply equal calcium; the citrate is only 3(40.08) ÷ 498.4 = 24.1% Ca against 40.0% for the carbonate. (C) forgets the subscript 3, taking one mole of citrate per mole of Ca. (D) multiplies 0.600 g by the fraction of Ca in the citrate (0.241) instead of dividing by it, which gives a mass smaller than the calcium it is supposed to contain.
parts.n: 1.1.A.3 and 1.3.A.3 (topic 1.1), skill 5.F. Thinking: go from mass of an element to moles, through the formula's subscript, to the mass of a different compound. Trap: (C), dropping the 3 in Ca₃.

parts.q:
A student analyzes two pure gas samples, each made only of sulfur and oxygen. Sample 1 is 49.9% oxygen by mass and sample 2 is 60.0% oxygen by mass. She claims that the results violate the law of definite proportions, since sulfur and oxygen combine in two different mass ratios. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) It is correct, because the law says two elements always combine in the same mass ratio, and these samples have two ratios.
(B) It is incorrect: the samples are two compounds, SO₂ and SO₃, and the law requires only that each compound have one fixed ratio.
(C) It is incorrect: the samples are two compounds, SO and S₂O₃, and the law requires only that each compound have one fixed ratio.
(D) It is correct, because sample 2 has 1.5 times as much oxygen per gram of sulfur as sample 1 does, when the law requires equal amounts.
parts.a: (B). Per 100 g, sample 1 has 50.1 g S (1.56 mol) and 49.9 g O (3.12 mol), a 1 : 2.00 ratio, so it is SO₂; sample 2 has 40.0 g S (1.25 mol) and 60.0 g O (3.75 mol), 1 : 3.01, so it is SO₃. Two pure samples with different compositions are two different compounds, and the law of definite proportions says only that every pure sample of one compound has the same composition. (A) misstates the law as a rule about pairs of elements rather than about a compound. (C) reads the mass ratios as atom ratios: 50.1 g : 49.9 g looks like SO and 40.0 g : 60.0 g like S₂O₃, but a sulfur atom has about twice the mass of an oxygen atom, so the masses must be turned into moles first. (D) quotes a true number (0.996 vs 1.500 g O per g S) but draws the wrong conclusion: a 3 : 2 ratio of small whole numbers is what two compounds with 2 and 3 O atoms per S atom give.
parts.n: 1.3.A.2 and 1.3.A.3 (topic 1.3), skill 6.D. Thinking: convert each composition to an empirical formula before judging whether the law is broken. Trap: (C), the right verdict with formulas read from mass ratios instead of mole ratios.

parts.q:
Two sealed flasks are described at the particle level. Flask 1 holds six identical molecules, each made of one nitrogen atom bonded to one oxygen atom. Flask 2 holds three N₂ molecules and three O₂ molecules. Which of the following correctly compares the contents of the two flasks?
(A) Both flasks hold pure substances, because each contains only nitrogen and oxygen atoms in a 1 : 1 ratio.
(B) Flask 1 holds a mixture and flask 2 a pure substance, because flask 2 contains only diatomic molecules.
(C) The flasks differ in percent nitrogen by mass, because in flask 2 no N atom is bonded to an O atom.
(D) Both are 46.7% nitrogen by mass, but only flask 1 is pure, so an elemental analysis cannot tell them apart.
parts.a: (D). Each flask holds 6 N atoms and 6 O atoms, so each is 14.01 ÷ (14.01 + 16.00) = 46.7% N by mass. Flask 1 has one kind of particle, NO molecules, so it is a pure substance; flask 2 has two kinds, N₂ and O₂, so it is a mixture. Because the elemental compositions are identical, an elemental analysis alone gives the same result for both. (A) counts atoms instead of kinds of particles: a pure substance has one kind of molecule or formula unit. (B) reverses the two flasks; being diatomic does not make N₂ and O₂ the same substance. (C) confuses bonding with composition: mass percent depends only on how many atoms of each element are present.
parts.n: 1.4.A.1 and 1.3.A.1 (topic 1.4), skill 4.C. Thinking: classify by kinds of particles, then check that a mixture and a compound can share an elemental composition. Trap: (A), which calls anything with a 1 : 1 atom ratio pure.

parts.q:
The photoelectron spectrum of an unknown gaseous species shows five peaks with relative heights 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 3, in order of decreasing binding energy. One student says the species is a phosphorus atom; another says it is an S⁺ ion. Which of the following would settle the question?
(A) Counting the peaks, since a P atom would show five peaks while an S⁺ ion, having lost an electron, would show only four.
(B) Comparing the peak heights with those expected, since P and S⁺ have different numbers of electrons in the 3p subshell.
(C) Comparing each peak's position with a P atom's spectrum, since S⁺ has 16 protons and would show every peak at higher energy.
(D) Checking that the 3p peak is lowest in energy, since in a cation the 3s electrons are the first ones removed, not the 3p.
parts.a: (C). P and S⁺ both have 15 electrons, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³, so their spectra have the same number of peaks with the same heights. They differ in nuclear charge, 15 versus 16, so S⁺ attracts every electron more strongly and each of its peaks lies at a higher binding energy than the matching peak of a P atom. (A) is wrong because S⁺ still has five occupied subshells; losing one of sulfur's four 3p electrons leaves three. (B) fails because both species have three 3p electrons, giving the same 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 3 pattern. (D) is false and would not help: the 3p electrons have the lowest binding energy in both species, and a cation of sulfur loses a 3p electron first.
parts.n: 1.6.A.1 and 1.5.A.3 (topic 1.6), skill 2.C. Thinking: peak heights report the configuration and peak positions report the nuclear charge, so only positions can separate two isoelectronic species. Trap: (A), assuming the ion loses a whole peak.

parts.q:
A student uses these data about three group 1 elements to argue that Coulomb's law does not apply to electrons in atoms.
Element · nuclear charge · core electrons · atomic radius (pm) · first ionization energy (kJ/mol)
Li · +3 · 2 · 152 · 520
Na · +11 · 10 · 186 · 496
K · +19 · 18 · 227 · 419
Argument: 'Attraction increases with charge. The nuclear charge rises from +3 to +19, so the valence electron should be held more tightly and the first ionization energy should rise. It falls, so Coulomb's law fails.' Which of the following identifies the flaw in the argument?
(A) It uses the full nuclear charge; the core electrons shield the valence electron, so the net charge it feels stays near +1 as its distance grows.
(B) It ignores the valence electrons: K has more valence electrons than Li, and their repulsion makes it easier to remove one of them.
(C) It treats ionization energy as a force; Coulomb's law describes forces only, so it cannot be used to reason about ionization energy.
(D) It ignores the neutrons: they add mass to the nucleus down the group, and a heavier nucleus pulls less strongly on the valence electron.
parts.a: (A). In each atom, the core electrons (2, 10 and 18) sit between the nucleus and the single valence electron and shield it, so the net charge it feels is roughly +3 − 2, +11 − 10 and +19 − 18, about +1 in each. Meanwhile the radius grows from 152 to 227 pm, and by Coulomb's law a similar charge at a greater distance attracts less, so the first ionization energy falls, as the data show. The data support Coulomb's law once shielding is included. (B) is false: every group 1 atom has one valence electron. (C) rejects a legitimate qualitative use: a weaker attraction means less energy is needed to remove the electron, which is how Coulomb's law explains ionization energy. (D) gives neutrons a role they do not have: they carry no charge, and mass plays no part in Coulombic attraction.
parts.n: 1.5.A.2 and 1.5.A.4 (topic 1.5), skill 6.D. Thinking: apply Coulomb's law with the net charge felt after shielding, and with distance. Trap: (C), which throws out the model instead of finding the missing factor.

parts.q:
The mass spectrum of a sample of bromine, recorded as singly charged Br⁺ ions, shows a peak at m/z 79 with relative height 100 and a peak at m/z 81 with relative height 97.3. The isotopic masses are 78.92 and 80.92 amu. A student calculates the average atomic mass.
Step 1: The m/z 79 peak is taller, so ⁷⁹Br carries more weight in the average.
Step 2: The fractional abundances are ⁷⁹Br = 100 ÷ 100 = 1.000 and ⁸¹Br = 97.3 ÷ 100 = 0.973.
Step 3: Weighted sum = 78.92(1.000) + 80.92(0.973) = 157.66 amu.
Step 4: Average atomic mass = 157.66 ÷ 2 = 78.83 amu.
Which of the following identifies the first error?
(A) Step 1, because the two peaks are so nearly equal in height that neither isotope should carry more weight than the other.
(B) Step 3, because the isotopic masses must be replaced by the mass numbers 79 and 81 before any weighting is done.
(C) Step 4, because the weighted sum from Step 3 should be divided by 197.3, the total of the peak heights, rather than by 2.
(D) Step 2, because heights relative to the tallest peak must be divided by their total, 197.3, giving 0.507 and 0.493.
parts.a: (D). Fractional abundances must add to 1, and 1.000 + 0.973 does not. Dividing each height by the total, 100 + 97.3 = 197.3, gives 0.507 for ⁷⁹Br and 0.493 for ⁸¹Br, and the average is 0.507(78.92) + 0.493(80.92) = 79.91 amu. The student's 78.83 amu is below the mass of the lighter isotope, which no average of the two can be. (A) objects to a correct step: 100 is greater than 97.3, so ⁷⁹Br is slightly more abundant and does carry slightly more weight. (B) would make the answer less precise, not correct it; isotopic masses are the right values to weight. (C) keeps the wrong fractions from Step 2 and gives 157.66 ÷ 197.3 = 0.799 amu, which is not a possible atomic mass.
parts.n: 1.2.A.2 (topic 1.2), skill 5.D. Thinking: check each step against what the quantity must be (fractions add to 1; an average lies between the isotope masses). Trap: (C), which spots a problem at Step 4 but misses its source.

fr.title: Rubidium chloride: identity and purity
fr.stem:
A white crystalline solid is known to be the chloride of a single group 1 metal, M. A sample of the metal extracted from the solid in bottle 1 gives a mass spectrum, recorded as singly charged M⁺ ions, with two peaks: m/z 85, relative height 100, and m/z 87, relative height 38.6. The isotopic masses are 84.91 amu and 86.91 amu.
A 1.000 g portion of the solid from bottle 1 contains 0.2932 g of chlorine. A 1.000 g portion of the solid from bottle 2, which carries the same label, contains 0.3100 g of chlorine.
Molar masses (g/mol): Na 22.99, K 39.10, Cl 35.45.

parts.q: Calculate the average atomic mass of M from the mass spectrum, and identify M.
parts.a: 85.47 amu, so M is rubidium. The heights are relative to the tallest peak, so each is divided by the total, 138.6: ⁸⁵M is 100/138.6 = 0.7215 and ⁸⁷M is 38.6/138.6 = 0.2785. Average = 0.7215(84.91) + 0.2785(86.91) = 85.47 amu (1 point). This matches rubidium, a group 1 metal (1 point).
parts.n: The unweighted mean, 85.91 amu, or a sum divided by 100 (118.5 amu), earns nothing for the calculation; an identification that does not follow from the calculated value earns nothing.

parts.q: Using the data for bottle 1, show that the solid has the formula MCl. Then explain, in terms of electron configuration, why M forms an ion with a charge of 1+.
parts.a: n(Cl) = 0.2932 g ÷ 35.45 g/mol = 8.271 × 10⁻³ mol. The rest of the 1.000 g is M: 0.7068 g ÷ 85.47 g/mol = 8.270 × 10⁻³ mol. The ratio is 1.000 : 1, so the formula is MCl (1 point). Rubidium is [Kr]5s¹: losing its single 5s electron leaves the krypton configuration, while a second electron would have to come from the n = 4 shell, much closer to the nucleus and far more strongly attracted, so Rb forms Rb⁺ (1 point).
parts.n: Using 1.000 g as the mass of M, or comparing masses rather than moles, earns nothing. 'It is in group 1' with no reference to the single valence electron and the next, inner shell earns nothing.

parts.q: One student claims that the solid in bottle 2 is RbCl that has absorbed water from the air. Another claims that it is RbCl mixed with some KCl. Which claim is consistent with the data? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Only the KCl claim. Pure RbCl is 35.45 ÷ 120.92 = 29.32% Cl, and bottle 2 is 31.00% Cl, higher. Water contains no chlorine, so absorbed water would dilute the chlorine and lower the percent below 29.32% (1 point). KCl is 35.45 ÷ 74.55 = 47.55% Cl, richer in chlorine than RbCl, so mixing it in raises the percent above 29.32%, as observed (1 point).
parts.n: Choosing the KCl claim without comparing percents of chlorine earns nothing. Agreeing with the water claim ('water adds mass') earns nothing, because added mass that contains no Cl can only lower the percent.

parts.q: Assuming that KCl is the only impurity, calculate the mass percent of RbCl in the solid from bottle 2.
parts.a: 90.8% RbCl. Let x be the mass fraction of RbCl: 29.32x + 47.55(1 − x) = 31.00 (1 point for this setup or an equivalent one in grams). Then 47.55 − 18.23x = 31.00, so x = 16.55 ÷ 18.23 = 0.908, or 90.8% RbCl and 9.2% KCl (1 point).
parts.n: The ratio 29.32 ÷ 31.00 = 94.6%, which ignores the chlorine the KCl supplies, earns nothing; so does 31.00 ÷ 29.32 = 106%, since a mass percent above 100% is impossible.

parts.q: A third student says the impurity might be NaCl instead, and that the chlorine analysis cannot tell KCl from NaCl. Do you agree? Justify your answer, and describe one additional measurement that would identify the impurity.
parts.a: Agree. Any impurity that is richer in chlorine than RbCl can raise the sample to 31.00% Cl: KCl (47.55% Cl) fits the data with 90.8% RbCl, and NaCl (60.66% Cl) fits with 94.6% RbCl, so the Cl percent alone cannot decide. Measuring the mass percent of potassium (or of sodium) would: a KCl impurity makes the sample 4.84% K and 0% Na, while an NaCl impurity makes it 2.11% Na and 0% K.
parts.n: Disagreeing, or proposing to repeat the chlorine analysis more carefully, earns nothing: both impurities fit the same chlorine result.

parts.q: The first ionization energy of potassium is 419 kJ/mol. Predict whether the first ionization energy of M is greater than or less than 419 kJ/mol, and justify your prediction using Coulomb's law.
parts.a: Less than 419 kJ/mol. Rubidium's valence electron is in the 5s subshell, farther from the nucleus than potassium's 4s electron. Rubidium's extra protons are matched by extra inner electrons that shield them, so the net charge the valence electron feels is similar, and by Coulomb's law the same charge at a greater distance attracts less, so less energy removes the electron.
parts.n: 'Greater, because Rb has more protons' earns nothing. 'Less, because it is lower in the group' with no reference to distance and shielding earns nothing.

fr.title: Copper sulfide: one compound or two?
fr.stem:
Two lab groups each heat a coil of copper wire with excess powdered sulfur in a covered crucible in a fume hood; excess sulfur burns off as SO₂(g). Each group cools the crucible and weighs the black solid product.
Group · mass of copper (g) · mass of product (g)
1 · 1.271 · 1.591
2 · 1.271 · 1.910
Molar masses (g/mol): Cu 63.55, S 32.07.

parts.q: Determine the empirical formula of group 1's product. Show your work.
parts.n: Using the product mass as the sulfur mass, or taking a ratio of masses (1.271 : 0.320 ≈ 4 : 1), earns nothing.

parts.q: Suppose some of the product had spattered out of group 1's crucible during heating. Predict whether the calculated ratio of S to Cu would be too high, too low, or unaffected, and justify your prediction.
parts.a: Too low. The mass of sulfur is found by difference, product − copper. Losing product makes the final mass too small, so the sulfur mass and moles of sulfur come out too small, while the moles of copper (from the wire's mass) are unchanged; S : Cu is therefore too low.
parts.n: A prediction with no reasoning, or 'too high because solid was lost', earns nothing.

parts.q: Group 2's product mass fits CuS. Their teacher suggests that group 2 may not have burned off all of the excess sulfur. Describe how group 2 could test this with their crucible, and state the result that would show that unreacted sulfur remained.
parts.a: Heat the crucible strongly again (lid ajar, in the hood), cool it and reweigh, repeating until the mass is constant. If the mass falls, toward about 1.59 g, free sulfur was still present and has burned off; if it stays at 1.910 g, the product holds no free sulfur.
parts.n: 'Repeat the experiment' or 'weigh it again' without reheating to constant mass earns nothing; a test with no stated result that would show excess sulfur earns nothing.

parts.q: A student concludes: 'Because the two groups used the same reactants and got different formulas, copper sulfide does not obey the law of definite proportions.' Evaluate the student's claim.
parts.a: The claim is not justified. The law applies to a pure compound: every pure sample of one compound has the same composition. Either group 2's solid is a mixture (Cu₂S with leftover sulfur), and a mixture's composition can vary, or the groups made two different compounds, Cu₂S and CuS, each with its own fixed composition. Neither case breaks the law.
parts.n: Agreeing with the student earns nothing. 'The law is always true' without explaining the two results earns nothing.

fr.title: Iron in a fortified cereal
fr.stem: A cereal box states that one 55 g serving provides 18 mg of iron, added as tiny particles of iron metal. To test the claim, a student crushes 50.0 g of the cereal, mixes it with water in a sealed bag, and stirs the slurry with a strong magnet for 10 minutes. She rinses the particles that cling to the magnet with water, dries them, and finds their mass to be 0.0120 g. Fe = 55.85 g/mol; Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.q: Calculate the mass of iron, in milligrams, that the student's result indicates for one 55 g serving.
parts.a: 13.2 mg. 0.0120 g ÷ 50.0 g of cereal × 55 g = 0.0132 g = 13.2 mg per serving.
parts.n: Reporting 12.0 mg (no scaling to 55 g), or dividing the wrong way (0.0109 g), earns nothing.

parts.q: Calculate the number of iron atoms in one serving if the label is correct.
parts.n: Using 18 g instead of 0.018 g (1.9 × 10²³), or dividing by Avogadro's number, earns nothing.

parts.q: The student claims that the manufacturer overstates the iron content. Evaluate the claim by identifying one source of error in the method and the direction in which it moves her result.
parts.a: The data do not support the claim. The magnet is unlikely to collect every particle: some iron stays trapped in the soggy cereal or is washed away in the rinse, so these losses make 13.2 mg a low estimate of the iron present. The shortfall from 18 mg may come from the method rather than the cereal, and one trial cannot settle the question.
parts.n: Agreeing because 13.2 < 18, or naming an error with no direction ('human error'), earns nothing.

parts.q: Describe a modification to the procedure that would test whether the magnet recovers all of the iron, and state the result that would show complete recovery.
parts.a: Add a known mass of iron powder, for example 0.0100 g, to a cereal known to contain no added iron, and process it in exactly the same way. If the mass recovered equals the mass added (within the balance's precision), the method recovers all the iron; a smaller recovery gives the fraction to correct for. (Stirring the same slurry a second time and recovering essentially no more iron is also acceptable.)
parts.n: 'Use a stronger magnet' or 'repeat the experiment' with no result that would show complete recovery earns nothing.

u4.intro: A periodic table and the AP Chemistry equations sheet are allowed, and a calculator may be used throughout.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-4 refer to the following.

A student is asked to find the mass percent of Na₂CO₃ in a white powder that is a mixture of Na₂CO₃ and NaCl only. She dissolves 2.500 g of the powder in about 50 mL of distilled water and adds 40.0 mL of 0.500 M CaCl₂(aq); a white precipitate of CaCO₃ forms. She collects the solid on a filter paper of mass 0.912 g, rinses it with distilled water, and then dries, cools and weighs it three times.
Weighing · mass of filter paper + solid (g)
After 1st drying · 2.614
After 2nd drying · 2.431
After 3rd drying · 2.429
Molar masses (g/mol): Na₂CO₃ 105.99, NaCl 58.44, CaCO₃ 100.09. All sodium salts are soluble in water; CaCO₃ is insoluble.

parts.q:
Which of the following is closest to the mass percent of Na₂CO₃ in the powder?
(A) 60.7%
(B) 64.3%
(C) 72.1%
(D) 84.8%
parts.a: (B). The mass must be read once the solid is dry: the 2nd and 3rd weighings agree (2.431 g and 2.429 g), so m(CaCO₃) = 2.429 − 0.912 = 1.517 g. n(CaCO₃) = 1.517 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 1.516 × 10⁻² mol, and each CO₃²⁻ came from one Na₂CO₃, so m(Na₂CO₃) = 1.516 × 10⁻² mol × 105.99 g/mol = 1.606 g, which is 1.606 ÷ 2.500 = 64.3% of the powder. (A) divides the mass of CaCO₃ by the sample mass, as if the precipitate were the Na₂CO₃ itself; the two compounds have different molar masses. (C) uses the first weighing, 1.702 g of solid, which still held water that the later dryings removed. (D) assumes that all 2.00 × 10⁻² mol of the added Ca²⁺ precipitated, but Ca²⁺ was in excess, so the carbonate, not the Ca²⁺, sets the mass of precipitate.
parts.n: 4.5.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: turn a constant-mass weighing into moles of precipitate, then go back through the 1:1 ratio to the analyte. Trap: (C), using the first weighing before the solid had reached constant mass.

parts.q:
Her lab partner proposes adding only 10.0 mL of the 0.500 M CaCl₂(aq) instead of 40.0 mL, to save reagent. Which of the following best evaluates the proposal?
(A) Acceptable, because a precipitation goes to completion, so even a small amount of CaCl₂ converts all of the carbonate to CaCO₃.
(B) Not acceptable, because unreacted Na₂CO₃ would be trapped in the solid, so the calculated percent would come out too high.
(C) Acceptable, because Ca²⁺ is a spectator ion, so the amount of CaCl₂ added does not change the mass of precipitate that forms.
(D) Not acceptable, because 10.0 mL supplies only 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol Ca²⁺, so the calculated percent would be about 21%, far too low.
parts.a: (D). 10.0 mL × 0.500 M = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol Ca²⁺, but the sample holds 1.52 × 10⁻² mol CO₃²⁻. Ca²⁺ would become the limiting reactant, only 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CaCO₃ could form, and the student would calculate 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol × 105.99 g/mol ÷ 2.500 g = 21.2% instead of 64.3%. A gravimetric analysis works only when the precipitating reagent is in excess, as the original 40.0 mL (2.00 × 10⁻² mol Ca²⁺) is. (A) confuses a reaction going to completion with every reactant being used up: the reaction stops when the limiting reactant runs out. (B) gets the direction wrong: leftover carbonate stays dissolved and passes into the filtrate, so the precipitate is too small, not too large. (C) misidentifies the spectators: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators, while Ca²⁺ is part of the precipitate.
parts.n: 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 2.F. Thinking: before trusting a gravimetric result, compare moles to check that the precipitating reagent is in excess. Trap: (A), which reads 'goes to completion' as 'uses up all of the analyte'.

parts.q:
Which test on a portion of the filtrate would confirm that enough CaCl₂ was added in the original procedure to precipitate all of the carbonate?
(A) Test the electrical conductivity of the filtrate; if it conducts, excess Ca²⁺ ions must still be dissolved in it.
(B) Evaporate the filtrate to dryness; if a white solid remains, all of the Na₂CO₃ was converted into CaCO₃.
(C) Add a few drops of Na₂CO₃(aq); if a white precipitate forms, Ca²⁺ is left over, so no carbonate remained.
(D) Check that the filtrate is clear and colorless; if no cloudiness appears, no carbonate is left in solution.
parts.a: (C). If adding more carbonate produces more CaCO₃, the filtrate still contains Ca²⁺, so Ca²⁺ was the excess reactant and CO₃²⁻ the limiting one: essentially every carbonate ion from the sample has been precipitated. (A) fails because the filtrate conducts whatever the outcome: it always contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the sample and from the CaCl₂. (B) fails for the same reason: NaCl is left when the filtrate evaporates, whether or not any carbonate remained. (D) fails because dissolved Na₂CO₃ is itself clear and colorless, so a clear filtrate says nothing about whether carbonate ions remain.
parts.n: 4.7.A.5 (topic 4.7), skill 2.C. Thinking: a useful test gives different results depending on whether the reagent was in excess; a test that always gives the same result proves nothing. Trap: (D), reading 'clear' as 'no carbonate'.

parts.q:
Which of the following ranks the dissolved ions in the filtrate from the greatest to the least number of moles?
(A) Cl⁻ > Na⁺ > Ca²⁺, with essentially no CO₃²⁻
(B) Na⁺ > Cl⁻ > Ca²⁺, with essentially no CO₃²⁻
(C) Na⁺ > Cl⁻ > CO₃²⁻, with essentially no Ca²⁺
(D) Cl⁻ > Na⁺, with essentially no Ca²⁺ or CO₃²⁻
parts.a: (A). The sample holds 1.606 g Na₂CO₃ (1.516 × 10⁻² mol) and 2.500 − 1.606 = 0.894 g NaCl (1.53 × 10⁻² mol). Na⁺ = 2(1.516 × 10⁻²) + 1.53 × 10⁻² = 4.56 × 10⁻² mol. Cl⁻ = 1.53 × 10⁻² from the NaCl + 2(2.00 × 10⁻²) from the CaCl₂ = 5.53 × 10⁻² mol. Ca²⁺ left = 2.00 × 10⁻² − 1.516 × 10⁻² = 4.8 × 10⁻³ mol, and the carbonate is all in the precipitate. (B) counts only one Cl⁻ per CaCl₂ (3.53 × 10⁻² mol in all) and so ranks Na⁺ first. (C) treats carbonate as the excess reactant, but Ca²⁺ was in excess. (D) assumes Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ were present in exactly equal amounts, so that both are used up; in fact Ca²⁺ exceeded the carbonate by 4.8 × 10⁻³ mol.
parts.n: 4.3.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.3), skill 1.B. Thinking: track every ion through a precipitation: spectators stay, the excess reactant's ion stays, the limiting one leaves. Trap: (B), counting one chloride per CaCl₂.

mc.stem:
Questions 5-8 refer to the following.

A student must identify an unknown white solid that is known to be one of four weak monoprotic acids, HA.
Acid · molar mass (g/mol)
Benzoic acid · 122.12
Phenylacetic acid · 136.15
Salicylic acid · 138.12
Cinnamic acid · 148.16
In each trial she weighs a sample of the acid into a flask, dissolves it in about 25 mL of distilled water, adds 2 drops of phenolphthalein, and titrates with 0.1000 M NaOH(aq) until a pale pink color lasts for 30 seconds.
Trial · mass of acid (g) · initial buret reading (mL) · final buret reading (mL) · color at the end
1 · 0.3120 · 0.50 · 23.10 · pale pink
2 · 0.2985 · 1.20 · 24.95 · deep magenta (NaOH was added quickly near the end)
3 · 0.3050 · 0.35 · 22.43 · pale pink

parts.q:
Which acid is the unknown most likely to be, and why?
(A) Salicylic acid, because trials 1 and 3 agree at 138.1 g/mol and trial 2 went past the endpoint
(B) Phenylacetic acid, because the mean of all three trials, 134.0 g/mol, is closest to 136.15 g/mol
(C) Benzoic acid, because trial 2 used the most NaOH, so its value of 125.7 g/mol is the most complete
(D) Salicylic acid, because trial 2 used the smallest mass of acid, so its result is the least reliable
parts.a: (A). Each trial gives M = mass ÷ mol NaOH, since HA and OH⁻ react 1:1. Trial 1: 22.60 mL × 0.1000 M = 2.260 × 10⁻³ mol, so M = 0.3120 g ÷ 2.260 × 10⁻³ mol = 138.1 g/mol. Trial 3: 22.08 mL gives 2.208 × 10⁻³ mol and 138.1 g/mol. Trial 2: 23.75 mL gives 2.375 × 10⁻³ mol and 125.7 g/mol. The deep magenta color shows excess NaOH was added past the endpoint, so trial 2's volume is too large and its molar mass too low; it should be rejected. Trials 1 and 3 agree to within 0.06%, and their mean, 138.1 g/mol, matches salicylic acid (138.12) and not phenylacetic acid (136.15), which is 1.4% away. (B) averages in a trial with a known error, and the bad value drags the mean down toward 136. (C) treats extra NaOH as a more complete reaction, but NaOH added after the endpoint has no acid left to react with. (D) names the right acid for the wrong reason: the sample mass is already accounted for in the calculation; the problem with trial 2 is the overshoot.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 (topic 4.6), skill 2.D. Thinking: compute each trial, use the lab notes to decide which trial to reject, then match the result against candidates that differ by little more than 1%. Trap: (B), averaging every trial by habit.

parts.q:
A classmate uses the same procedure on a sample of the same acid that had been left uncovered and had absorbed water from the air. He records the mass of the damp solid. How does this affect his calculated molar mass?
(A) Too low, because the water dilutes the acid, so less NaOH is needed to reach the endpoint
(B) Too low, because the water in the sample also reacts with NaOH, so more NaOH is needed
(C) Too high, because the recorded mass includes water that does not react with the NaOH
(D) Unchanged, because the sample is dissolved in water before the titration in any case
parts.a: (C). The titration counts only the moles of HA actually present, and a damp sample holds fewer moles of HA than its recorded mass suggests. The calculation divides the full recorded mass (acid + water) by those moles, so the molar mass comes out too high. (A) is right that less NaOH is needed, but fewer moles in the denominator make the quotient larger, not smaller. (B) treats water as an acid that consumes a measurable amount of NaOH; the endpoint marks the neutralization of HA, and water is the solvent in every trial. (D) confuses the water added to dissolve the sample, which changes nothing, with water weighed as if it were acid, which inflates the mass.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.6), skill 6.G. Thinking: trace the error through M = mass ÷ moles: which quantity is wrong, and in which direction? Trap: (A), which gets 'less NaOH' right but divides the wrong way.

parts.q:
Each buret reading is uncertain by ±0.02 mL, so each titrant volume is uncertain by about ±0.04 mL. Which change to the procedure would most reduce the percent uncertainty in the titrant volume?
(A) Dissolve each sample in 100 mL of water instead of 25 mL, so that the endpoint is easier to see
(B) Use about 0.60 g of acid per trial, so that each titration needs about 43 mL of the NaOH
(C) Titrate with 0.5000 M NaOH instead of 0.1000 M, so that each trial uses less solution
(D) Use about 0.10 g of acid per trial, so that each titration needs only about 7 mL of NaOH
parts.a: (B). Percent uncertainty = ±0.04 mL ÷ volume delivered, so the larger the titrant volume, the smaller the percent uncertainty. The present trials use about 22.6 mL (0.18%). Doubling the acid to 0.60 g needs 0.60 ÷ 138.1 = 4.3 × 10⁻³ mol NaOH, or 43.4 mL, which still fits in a 50 mL buret and halves the percent uncertainty to 0.09%. (A) changes nothing about the moles of acid, so the volume of NaOH, and its uncertainty, are unchanged. (C) cuts the volume to about 4.5 mL, raising the uncertainty to about 0.9%. (D) cuts the volume to about 7.2 mL, raising it to about 0.6%.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 (topic 4.6), skill 2.C. Thinking: a fixed reading uncertainty matters less when the measured volume is larger. Trap: (C), which confuses a quicker titration with a more precise one.

parts.q:
A student writes the net ionic equation for the titration reaction as H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), with Na⁺ and A⁻ as spectator ions. Which of the following best evaluates this equation?
(A) It is correct, because every reaction between an acid and a hydroxide has this net ionic equation.
(B) It is incorrect, because Na⁺ combines with A⁻ to form a solid salt, which must appear as a product.
(C) It is correct, because HA ionizes completely once OH⁻ is added, so H⁺ is the species that reacts.
(D) It is incorrect, because HA is a weak acid that is mostly un-ionized and donates its proton to OH⁻.
parts.a: (D). A weak acid exists in solution mostly as HA molecules, so HA itself is the proton donor: HA(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → A⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). HA and A⁻ are a conjugate acid-base pair, as are H₂O and OH⁻. A⁻ is a product of the reaction, not a spectator, and only Na⁺ is a spectator. (A) holds only for strong acids, which exist as H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and A⁻ before any base is added. (B) contradicts the solubility of sodium salts: NaA stays dissolved as Na⁺ and A⁻. (C) describes the result of the reaction as if it came first: OH⁻ removes the proton from HA in the reaction itself; HA does not first ionize fully on its own.
parts.n: 4.2.A.3 and 4.8.A.1 (topic 4.8), skill 5.E. Thinking: decide what species actually carries the proton in solution before writing the net ionic equation. Trap: (A), the strong-acid equation applied to every neutralization.

mc.stem:
Questions 9-12 refer to the following.

A student places 40.0 mL of Ba(OH)₂(aq) of unknown concentration in a beaker fitted with a conductivity probe and adds 0.0500 M H₂SO₄(aq) from a buret, recording the electrical conductivity of the mixture after each addition. A white solid, BaSO₄, forms from the first drop onward. BaSO₄ is insoluble in water; treat Ba(OH)₂ as fully dissociated into Ba²⁺ and OH⁻, and H₂SO₄ as supplying 2 H⁺ and 1 SO₄²⁻ per formula unit.
Volume of H₂SO₄ added (mL) · conductivity (µS/cm)
0.00 · 4450
2.00 · 3180
4.00 · 2020
6.00 · 970
8.00 · 12
10.00 · 1460
12.00 · 2810
A graph of conductivity against volume is two straight lines that meet at 8.00 mL.

parts.q:
What is the concentration of the Ba(OH)₂(aq)?
(A) 0.00500 M
(B) 0.00833 M
(C) 0.0100 M
(D) 0.0200 M
parts.a: (C). The conductivity reaches its minimum when the acid has exactly consumed the base: 8.00 mL × 0.0500 M = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol H₂SO₄. The net reaction is Ba²⁺ + 2 OH⁻ + 2 H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s) + 2 H₂O(l), so H₂SO₄ and Ba(OH)₂ react 1:1, and 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 0.0400 L = 0.0100 M. (A) halves the answer by counting only one H⁺ per H₂SO₄, as if two H₂SO₄ were needed for each Ba(OH)₂. (B) divides by the total volume at the equivalence point, 48.0 mL, instead of the 40.0 mL of base originally present. (D) doubles the answer by counting the 2 H⁺ per H₂SO₄ but forgetting the 2 OH⁻ per Ba(OH)₂.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 and 4.5.A.3 (topic 4.6), skill 5.D. Thinking: read the equivalence point from where the lines meet, then use the 1:1 ratio that the charges set. Trap: (D), counting the acid's two protons but not the base's two hydroxides.

parts.q:
The student repeats the experiment with 40.0 mL of the same Ba(OH)₂(aq), but titrates it with 0.0500 M HCl(aq) instead of 0.0500 M H₂SO₄(aq). BaCl₂ is soluble in water. Which prediction about the minimum of the conductivity graph is correct?
(A) The minimum would be at 16.0 mL and well above zero, because Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved.
(B) The minimum would be at 16.0 mL and near zero, because all of the OH⁻ is still converted to water.
(C) The minimum would be at 8.00 mL and well above zero, because Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved.
(D) The minimum would be at 8.00 mL and near zero, because H⁺ and OH⁻ still combine to form water.
parts.a: (A). The base holds 2 × 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol OH⁻, and HCl supplies only one H⁺ per formula unit, so the equivalence point needs 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 0.0500 M = 16.0 mL. The only net reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; no solid forms, so at the minimum the solution still holds 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol Ba²⁺ and 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol Cl⁻ and conducts well. (B) gets the volume right but forgets that removing OH⁻ leaves Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ behind. (C) gets the reason right but treats HCl as supplying as many H⁺ per formula unit as H₂SO₄ does. (D) repeats the original result without accounting for either change.
parts.n: 4.2.A.3 and 4.7.A.5 (topic 4.2), skill 2.B. Thinking: write the new net ionic equation, then ask which ions it removes and which it leaves behind. Trap: (B), expecting every neutralization to drive the conductivity to zero.

parts.q:
A student claims that the conductivity falls between 0 and 8.00 mL mainly because the added acid dilutes the solution. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?
(A) The claim is supported, because conductivity depends on the concentration of ions, and each addition lowers it.
(B) The claim is not supported, because H₂SO₄ is a strong electrolyte, so adding it can only add ions to the solution.
(C) The claim is partly supported: dilution explains the fall before 8.00 mL, and the added ions explain the rise after.
(D) The claim is not supported: by 8.00 mL the volume has grown by only 20%, yet the conductivity fell by over 99%.
parts.a: (D). Dilution alone from 40.0 mL to 48.0 mL would lower the ion concentrations only to 40.0/48.0 of their values, about 17%, but the conductivity falls from 4450 to 12 µS/cm. Nearly all of the ions must be leaving the solution: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ as solid BaSO₄, and H⁺ and OH⁻ as H₂O. The rise after 8.00 mL, while the solution keeps getting more dilute, confirms that dilution is not what controls the conductivity. (A) is true in general but cannot explain a 99% fall from a 20% volume change. (B) reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason: the added ions do not stay in solution before 8.00 mL; they are removed along with the base's ions. (C) accepts dilution as the cause of the fall, which the size of the fall rules out.
parts.n: 4.2.A.3 and 4.3.A.1 (topic 4.2), skill 6.B. Thinking: test a proposed cause against the size of the effect it would produce. Trap: (C), which sounds balanced but keeps the dilution explanation.

parts.q:
Suppose a particulate diagram of the original 40.0 mL of Ba(OH)₂(aq) shows 4 Ba²⁺ ions and 8 OH⁻ ions (water molecules not shown). Which of the following describes the diagram after 4.00 mL of the H₂SO₄(aq) has been added?
(A) 4 Ba²⁺, 4 OH⁻ and 2 SO₄²⁻ ions dissolved, and no solid
(B) 2 Ba²⁺ and 4 OH⁻ ions dissolved, and 2 formula units of solid BaSO₄
(C) 2 Ba²⁺, 4 OH⁻ and 4 H⁺ ions dissolved, and 2 formula units of solid BaSO₄
(D) 4 Ba²⁺, 8 OH⁻, 4 H⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻ ions dissolved, and no solid
parts.a: (B). 4.00 mL is half of the 8.00 mL needed, so the acid added corresponds to 2 H₂SO₄ for the 4 Ba(OH)₂ drawn: 4 H⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻. The 4 H⁺ combine with 4 OH⁻ to form water, and the 2 SO₄²⁻ combine with 2 Ba²⁺ to form 2 BaSO₄(s), leaving 2 Ba²⁺ and 4 OH⁻ dissolved, a neutral set. (A) treats Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ as spectators, but the stem says BaSO₄ is insoluble and forms from the first drop. (C) shows the precipitation but not the neutralization; H⁺ and OH⁻ cannot both remain, and the ions drawn carry a net +4 charge. (D) assumes nothing reacts until the equivalence point; in fact each addition reacts as it goes in.
parts.n: 4.3.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.3), skill 1.B. Thinking: scale the added acid to the drawn particles, apply both parts of the reaction, and check that the leftovers are neutral. Trap: (A), treating the barium and sulfate as spectator ions.

mc.stem:
Questions 13-15 refer to the following.

An older type of breath-alcohol tester bubbles a measured volume of breath through an acidified solution of potassium dichromate. Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) is converted to green Cr³⁺(aq) while ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is converted to acetic acid, CH₃COOH, and the tester measures how much green Cr³⁺ forms. A student balanced the equation for acidic solution as follows.
Step 1: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14 H⁺ + 6 e⁻ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 7 H₂O
Step 2: C₂H₅OH + H₂O → CH₃COOH + 4 H⁺ + 2 e⁻
Step 3: Multiply step 2 by 3, so that both half-reactions involve 6 e⁻.
Step 4: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3 C₂H₅OH + 2 H⁺ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 3 CH₃COOH + 4 H₂O

parts.q:
In which step does the student's work first go wrong?
(A) Step 1, because each Cr changes by 3, so the half-reaction should show 3 e⁻ rather than 6 e⁻
(B) Step 2, because its charges do not balance: the left side is neutral but the right side is +2
(C) Step 3, because the half-reactions must be scaled so that the numbers of H⁺, not of e⁻, match
(D) Step 4, because the H⁺ and H₂O were cancelled wrongly, leaving the equation unbalanced for charge
parts.a: (B). Step 1 is correct: two Cr atoms each go from +6 to +3, so 6 e⁻ are gained, and the charges balance (−2 + 14 − 6 = +6 = 2 × +3). Step 2 balances C, H and O, but its right side carries 4(+1) + 2(−1) = +2 against 0 on the left; it needs 4 e⁻, since carbon's average oxidation number rises from −2 to 0 for each of the two C atoms. Steps 3 and 4 then follow correctly from the faulty step 2, which is why step 4 is atom-balanced but carries 0 on the left and +6 on the right. (A) counts the change for one Cr atom and forgets that Cr₂O₇²⁻ contains two. (C) misstates the rule: half-reactions are scaled so that electrons lost equal electrons gained. (D) points to the step where the charge imbalance first shows, but the cancelling in step 4 was done correctly; the error was inherited from step 2.
parts.n: 4.9.A.1 and 4.2.A.2 (topic 4.9), skill 5.E. Thinking: check each step for both atom and charge balance, and separate where an error starts from where it becomes visible. Trap: (D), blaming the step where the imbalance appears.

parts.q:
For one breath sample the tester finds that 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol of Cr³⁺ formed. Using a correctly balanced equation, what mass of ethanol (46.07 g/mol) was in the sample?
(A) 2.76 mg
(B) 3.69 mg
(C) 2.07 mg
(D) 4.15 mg
parts.a: (C). With 4 e⁻ in the ethanol half-reaction, the electrons balance at 12: 2 Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3 C₂H₅OH + 16 H⁺ → 4 Cr³⁺ + 3 CH₃COOH + 11 H₂O. So 4 mol Cr³⁺ form for every 3 mol ethanol: 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 3/4 = 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol ethanol, and 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 46.07 g/mol = 2.07 × 10⁻³ g = 2.07 mg. (D) uses the student's step 4 ratio of 2 Cr³⁺ to 3 ethanol, giving 9.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol and 4.15 mg. (A) assumes one ethanol per Cr³⁺. (B) inverts the correct ratio, taking 4/3 instead of 3/4 (8.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol, 3.69 mg).
parts.n: 4.9.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: rebalance by electrons, then use the product-to-reactant mole ratio. Trap: (D), trusting the student's unbalanced equation.

parts.q:
A classmate claims that the orange-to-green color change shows that the dichromate ion lost electrons. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) Incorrect, because chromium goes from +6 to +3, so it gains electrons, which come from the carbon in ethanol.
(B) Correct, because chromium goes from +6 in Cr₂O₇²⁻ to +3 in Cr³⁺, and a drop in oxidation number is a loss.
(C) Incorrect, because chromium goes from +12 to +3, so each Cr atom gains 9 electrons from the ethanol.
(D) Incorrect, because the color change comes from the H⁺ that reacts, so this is an acid-base reaction.
parts.a: (A). In Cr₂O₇²⁻, 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so each Cr is +6; in Cr³⁺ it is +3. A decrease in oxidation number means electrons were gained, and they come from carbon, whose average oxidation number rises from −2 in ethanol to 0 in acetic acid. (B) has the right oxidation numbers but the wrong direction: losing negative electrons makes an oxidation number rise, not fall. (C) forgets that the ion contains two Cr atoms and assigns the whole +12 to one of them. (D) is wrong because oxidation numbers change; H⁺ is consumed in the balanced equation, but that does not make the reaction an acid-base reaction.
parts.n: 4.7.A.3 and 4.7.A.4 (topic 4.7), skill 6.D. Thinking: assign oxidation numbers, then connect their direction of change to the direction of electron transfer. Trap: (B), which equates a drop in oxidation number with a loss of electrons.

mc.stem:
Questions 16-18 refer to the following.

A student carries out four processes and records these observations.
Process · observations
1. Solid iodine, I₂, is warmed gently in a sealed tube · purple vapor fills the tube; dark crystals form on the cool top of the tube; the total mass does not change
2. Solid ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl, is heated at the bottom of an open test tube · the white solid disappears from the hot bottom and a white solid forms near the cool mouth; the gas in the hot part of the tube contains NH₃ and HCl molecules
3. Solid ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, is stirred into water · the solid disappears and the temperature falls from 22 °C to 9 °C; evaporating the water leaves white crystals identical to the starting solid
4. 2.470 g of pure copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃, a green solid, is heated strongly · a colorless gas identified as CO₂ is given off; 1.590 g of a black solid remains, and its mass does not change on further heating
Molar masses (g/mol): CuCO₃ 123.56, CuO 79.55, Cu₂O 143.09, Cu 63.55

parts.q:
In processes 1 and 2 a solid disappears from a hot region and a solid forms again in a cooler region. Which of the following best explains the difference between the two processes at the particle level?
(A) In both, only the attractions between particles are overcome, because in both the same solid re-forms on cooling.
(B) In 1, the covalent I–I bonds break to give I atoms; in 2, NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ ions leave the solid intact as gas particles.
(C) In both, chemical bonds are broken, because heating supplies energy and energy is needed to break any bond.
(D) In 1, I₂ molecules move apart intact; in 2, a proton moves from NH₄⁺ to Cl⁻, so covalent bonds break and form.
parts.a: (D). Process 1 is sublimation: the vapor is still I₂, so only the dispersion forces between molecules were overcome, a physical change. In process 2 the hot gas contains NH₃ and HCl, which are not in the solid: an N–H bond in NH₄⁺ broke and an H–Cl bond formed as the proton moved to Cl⁻, a chemical change that reverses on cooling. (A) judges by the end result only; the same solid re-forming does not show that no new substances existed in between, and the gas analysis shows they did. (B) reverses the evidence: purple I₂ vapor is molecular, and the gas in 2 is NH₃ and HCl, not ions. (C) treats all heating as bond breaking; warming iodine supplies enough energy to separate molecules, not to break I–I bonds.
parts.n: 4.4.A.1 (topic 4.4), skill 6.C. Thinking: identify which interactions change by asking what particles are present before and after, not what the change looks like. Trap: (A), classifying both by the solid that re-forms.

parts.q:
Which observation in the table is the WEAKEST evidence that a new substance formed in that process?
(A) The detection of NH₃ and HCl molecules in the hot part of the tube in process 2
(B) The colorless gas identified as CO₂ that is given off when CuCO₃ is heated in process 4
(C) The fall in temperature from 22 °C to 9 °C when NH₄NO₃ dissolves in water in process 3
(D) The black solid of constant mass that remains after CuCO₃ is heated in process 4
parts.a: (C). A temperature change is possible evidence of a chemical change, but in process 3 the table shows that evaporation returns crystals identical to the starting NH₄NO₃, so no new substance formed; the temperature fell because separating the ions from the lattice took in more energy than the ion-dipole attractions to water released. (A) is strong evidence: NH₃ and HCl are different substances from NH₄Cl. (B) is strong evidence: CO₂ was not present as a substance in the green solid. (D) is strong evidence: a new color and a new, constant mass show that a different solid remains.
parts.n: 4.1.A.1 and 4.1.A.2 (topic 4.1), skill 6.B. Thinking: weigh each observation against the other evidence recorded for the same process. Trap: (D), because a color change can occur without a reaction; here the constant new mass rules that out.

parts.q:
Which conclusion about the black solid in process 4 do the mass data best support?
(A) The black solid is Cu, formed as both CO₂ and oxygen are driven off.
(B) The black solid is CuO, formed as CO₂ is driven off.
(C) The black solid is CuO mixed with some unreacted CuCO₃.
(D) The black solid is Cu₂O, formed as CO₂ and some O₂ are driven off.
parts.a: (B). 2.470 g ÷ 123.56 g/mol = 1.999 × 10⁻² mol CuCO₃, and each formula unit keeps its one Cu atom. As CuO it would weigh 1.999 × 10⁻² mol × 79.55 g/mol = 1.590 g, exactly the mass found; the 0.880 g lost is 1.999 × 10⁻² mol of CO₂. (A) would leave 1.999 × 10⁻² mol × 63.55 g/mol = 1.270 g. (D) would leave 1.999 × 10⁻² ÷ 2 = 9.995 × 10⁻³ mol Cu₂O, or 1.430 g. (C) would weigh more than 1.590 g, and its mass would keep falling on further heating as the CuCO₃ decomposed; the table says the mass stayed constant.
parts.n: 4.5.A.1 and 4.1.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 6.B. Thinking: conserve copper atoms, compute the mass each candidate would leave, and compare with the data. Trap: (C), which overlooks that a mass that stays constant on reheating means the decomposition was complete.

mc.stem:
Questions 19-21 refer to the following.

In one airbag design, an electrical signal heats solid sodium azide, NaN₃, which decomposes in about 30 milliseconds:
Reaction 1: 2 NaN₃(s) → 2 Na(s) + 3 N₂(g)
The sodium metal formed is dangerous, so the charge also contains excess KNO₃, which reacts with it:
Reaction 2: 10 Na(s) + 2 KNO₃(s) → K₂O(s) + 5 Na₂O(s) + N₂(g)
The bag must fill to 60.0 L at 1.10 atm and 27 °C. Use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) and NaN₃ = 65.01 g/mol, and treat N₂ as an ideal gas.

parts.q:
Counting only the N₂ from reaction 1, what mass of NaN₃ is needed to fill the bag?
(A) 116 g
(B) 174 g
(C) 261 g
(D) 1.29 × 10³ g
parts.a: (A). n(N₂) = PV/RT = (1.10 atm)(60.0 L) ÷ [(0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K))(300. K)] = 2.68 mol.
