(B) is what an estimate from average bond enthalpies would say, but average values ignore the small differences between the same bond in different molecules; the ΔH°f values are measured and show a real difference. (D) brings in dispersion forces, which are not overcome in a reaction between gases, and it gets the direction wrong.
parts.n: 6.8.A.1 (topic 6.8), skill 6.D. Thinking: with identical products, the fuel that starts lower in enthalpy has less energy to release. Trap: (A), the sign of the reactant term.

mc.stem:
Questions 9-11 refer to the following.

A student measures the molar enthalpy of fusion of ice. She puts 100.0 g of water at 35.0 °C in a foam cup, adds ice cubes at 0.0 °C that she has patted dry, stirs until all of the ice has melted, and records the lowest temperature reached, 10.6 °C. Weighing the cup again shows that 27.0 g of ice was added. Assume that no heat is exchanged with the cup or the room. Specific heat capacity of liquid water = 4.18 J/(g·°C); molar mass of H₂O = 18.02 g/mol.

parts.q:
Which value of the molar enthalpy of fusion of ice, ΔH_fus, do the student's data give?
(A) 6.81 kJ/mol
(B) 6.01 kJ/mol
(C) 7.85 kJ/mol
(D) 3.85 kJ/mol
parts.a: (B). The warm water loses 100.0 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × (35.0 − 10.6) °C = 10 199 J. That heat does two jobs: it melts the ice, and then it warms the 27.0 g of meltwater from 0.0 °C to 10.6 °C, which takes 27.0 × 4.18 × 10.6 = 1196 J. So melting took 10 199 − 1196 = 9003 J for 27.0 ÷ 18.02 = 1.498 mol of ice, and ΔH_fus = 9003 J ÷ 1.498 mol = 6.01 kJ/mol. (A) credits all 10 199 J to melting and forgets that the meltwater also warmed. (C) uses 127.0 g as the mass that cooled from 35.0 °C, but only the original 100.0 g started warm. (D) uses 100.0 g in place of 27.0 g for the meltwater that warmed from 0.0 °C.
parts.n: 6.5.A.1 and 6.4.A.1 (topic 6.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: split the heat that the warm water gives up between the phase change and the warming of the meltwater. Trap: (A), which counts all of the heat as melting.

parts.q:
Which of the following mistakes would make the student's calculated ΔH_fus greater than the true value?
(A) The ice cubes still had a film of liquid water on them, which was weighed as part of the ice
(B) She recorded the final temperature a little before the last of the ice had melted
(C) Her thermometer reads 0.5 °C too high at every temperature, including the final one
(D) The ice came straight from a freezer at −18 °C, but she treated it as if it were at 0.0 °C
parts.a: (D). Ice at −18 °C must first be warmed to 0.0 °C, and that uses some of the heat the warm water gives up. The student credits that heat to melting, so she overestimates ΔH_fus (the same procedure with ice from −18 °C gives about 6.7 kJ/mol). (A) Part of the 27.0 g was already liquid, so less ice melted than she assumes; dividing the melting heat by too many moles makes ΔH_fus too low. (B) While ice remains, the temperature is still falling, so her reading is too high; the warm water then seems to have lost less heat and the meltwater to have gained more, so ΔH_fus comes out too low. (C) A thermometer that reads 0.5 °C high leaves the warm water's ΔT unchanged, but it makes the meltwater's rise from the assumed 0.0 °C look 0.5 °C larger, so slightly less heat is left for melting and ΔH_fus comes out a little low, not high.
parts.n: 6.5.A.1 and 6.4.A.2 (topic 6.5), skill 6.G. Thinking: follow each mistake through the energy balance to see whether the heat credited to melting rises or falls. Trap: (A), where extra water feels like extra heat.

parts.q:
A classmate adds 50.0 g of ice at 0.0 °C to 100.0 g of water at 35.0 °C in the same kind of cup. Using ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol, which of the following best describes the final state of the cup's contents?
(A) All liquid at about −3.3 °C, because the ice absorbs more heat than the warm water can supply
(B) All liquid at about 23.3 °C, because the mixture settles at the mass-weighted average temperature
(C) Ice and liquid water together at 0.0 °C, with about 6 g of the ice still unmelted
(D) All liquid at 0.0 °C, because the water cools only until the last of the ice has just melted
parts.a: (C). Cooling 100.0 g of water from 35.0 °C to 0.0 °C releases 100.0 × 4.18 × 35.0 = 14 630 J. Melting all 50.0 g of ice would take (50.0 ÷ 18.02) × 6010 J = 16 676 J, more than is available, so the water reaches 0.0 °C before all the ice has melted, and the temperature cannot fall further while ice and liquid are both present. The heat available melts (14 630 ÷ 6010) × 18.02 = 43.9 g, leaving about 6.1 g of ice. (A) is what the energy balance gives if all the ice is assumed to melt, but liquid water in contact with melting ice cannot be at −3.3 °C. (B) ignores the enthalpy of fusion and simply averages the temperatures. (D) would be true only if the heat available exactly matched the heat needed to melt the ice; here it falls about 2.0 kJ short.
parts.n: 6.5.A.1 and 6.5.A.2 (topic 6.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: compare the heat available with the heat needed before assuming that all of the ice melts. Trap: (A), the unchecked energy balance.

mc.stem:
Questions 12-15 refer to the following.

Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄(s), is white; the hydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O(s), is blue. The enthalpy change of the hydration reaction CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) cannot be measured directly in a calorimeter, because liquid water added to the solid dissolves some of it instead of forming only the hydrate. A student instead dissolves each solid in water in a foam-cup calorimeter:
Experiment 1: CuSO₄(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq), ΔH₁
Experiment 2: CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 5 H₂O(l), ΔH₂
Experiment · solid (molar mass) · mass of solid · mass of water · initial T (°C) · final T (°C)
1 · CuSO₄ (159.61 g/mol) · 5.00 g · 50.0 g · 21.0 · 30.1
2 · CuSO₄·5H₂O (249.69 g/mol) · 5.00 g · 50.0 g · 21.0 · 20.0
Assume that each solution has a mass of 55.0 g and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g·°C), and that the cup absorbs no heat.

parts.q:
Based on the student's data, which of the following is ΔH for CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)?
(A) −78.3 kJ/mol
(B) −55.3 kJ/mol
(C) +78.3 kJ/mol
(D) −124 kJ/mol
parts.a: (A). Experiment 1: q = 55.0 × 4.18 × 9.1 = 2092 J released by 5.00 ÷ 159.61 = 0.03133 mol, so ΔH₁ = −66.8 kJ/mol. Experiment 2: q = 55.0 × 4.18 × 1.0 = 230 J absorbed by 5.00 ÷ 249.69 = 0.02002 mol, so ΔH₂ = +11.5 kJ/mol. The target equation is equation 1 plus the reverse of equation 2: the aqueous ions cancel and the 5 H₂O(l) move to the reactant side. So ΔH = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂ = −66.8 − 11.5 = −78.3 kJ/mol. (B) adds the two values without reversing equation 2. (C) reverses the wrong equation, giving ΔH₂ − ΔH₁. (D) multiplies ΔH₂ by 5 because of the 5 H₂O, but equation 2 already contains the 5 H₂O and is used once.
parts.n: 6.9.B.2 and 6.4.A.1 (topic 6.9), skill 5.F. Thinking: turn each temperature change into a molar ΔH, then combine the equations so that the aqueous ions cancel. Trap: (B), adding without reversing.

parts.q:
An energy diagram for this system has three levels: CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(l), drawn at 0 kJ; CuSO₄·5H₂O(s); and the aqueous ions, Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 5 H₂O(l). Using ΔH₁ = −66.8 kJ/mol and ΔH₂ = +11.5 kJ/mol, where should the other two levels be drawn, per mole of copper(II) sulfate?
(A) Aqueous ions at −66.8 kJ; CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) at −55.3 kJ
(B) Aqueous ions at −66.8 kJ; CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) at −78.3 kJ
(C) CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) at −66.8 kJ; aqueous ions at −78.3 kJ
(D) Aqueous ions at +66.8 kJ; CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) at +78.3 kJ
parts.a: (B). Dissolving the anhydrous solid is exothermic, so the aqueous ions lie 66.8 kJ below the starting level, at −66.8 kJ. Dissolving the hydrate is endothermic, so the hydrate lies 11.5 kJ below the aqueous ions, at −78.3 kJ, the lowest of the three levels; that is why the hydration step, from 0 to −78.3 kJ, is exothermic. (A) puts the hydrate 11.5 kJ above the ions, which would make dissolving the hydrate exothermic. (C) swaps the two levels, putting the hydrate where the ions belong. (D) flips every sign, as if the temperature rise in experiment 1 meant that the system gained energy.
parts.n: 6.2.A.1 and 6.9.A.1 (topic 6.2), skill 1.B. Thinking: place each level from the sign and size of the step that leads to it, and check that the diagram reproduces both measurements. Trap: (A), the hydrate drawn above the ions.

parts.q:
The student's bottle of anhydrous CuSO₄ had been left open, and the solid had turned pale blue by absorbing water from the air. She used it for experiment 1, still treating it as pure CuSO₄ (159.61 g/mol). How would this affect the ΔH she calculates for the hydration reaction?
(A) More negative, because the water in the solid adds its own heat of hydration to the measurement
(B) Unchanged, because 5.00 g of the solid still contains the same number of moles of CuSO₄
(C) More negative, because a partly hydrated solid dissolves faster and so loses less heat to the room
(D) Less negative, because the solid releases less heat as it dissolves, so ΔH₁ is less negative
parts.a: (D). Part of the solid is already CuSO₄·5H₂O, whose dissolving absorbs heat rather than releasing it, and part of the 5.00 g is water, so fewer moles of CuSO₄ are present. The sample releases less heat than 5.00 g of pure CuSO₄ would, but she still divides by 0.03133 mol, so ΔH₁ comes out less negative. Because ΔH(hydration) = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂, it is less negative too. (A) gets the direction wrong: the hydration already happened in the bottle, so its heat is missing from the measurement, not added to it. (B) is false: some of the 5.00 g is water, so it contains fewer moles of CuSO₄. (C) confuses rate with the amount of heat; the partly hydrated solid simply has less heat to release.
parts.n: 6.9.B.1 and 6.4.A.7 (topic 6.9), skill 6.G. Thinking: trace a contaminated sample through the measured ΔH₁ and then through the Hess's law combination. Trap: (A), which counts the missing heat as extra.

parts.q:
A student notices that the anhydrous solid dissolves exothermically while the hydrate dissolves endothermically. She concludes that the Cu²⁺ ions must be attracted less strongly to water molecules in the solution made from the hydrate. Which of the following best evaluates her conclusion?
(A) She is correct, because an endothermic dissolving shows that the ion–water attractions formed are weaker
(B) She is correct, because breaking the covalent bonds between Cu²⁺ and water in the hydrate absorbs energy
(C) She is incorrect: both form the same hydrated ions, but in the hydrate water is already held by Cu²⁺
(D) She is incorrect: the hydrate absorbs heat only because 5.00 g of it contains fewer moles of CuSO₄
parts.a: (C). Both experiments end with the same solution of hydrated Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions, so the ion–water attractions in the final state are the same. The difference is in the starting solids: in CuSO₄·5H₂O, water molecules are already held to Cu²⁺ by ion–dipole attractions, so the energy those attractions release was released when the hydrate formed (the −78.3 kJ/mol of hydration). Dissolving the hydrate forms few new attractions but must still separate the ions, so it absorbs a little energy. (A) judges the attractions in the solution from ΔH alone, without noticing that the two processes start from different states. (B) calls the ion–water attractions covalent bonds, and in any case says nothing about the attractions in the solution. (D) confuses the amount of heat with its sign: fewer moles would mean less heat, but ΔH₂ is positive per mole.
parts.n: 6.1.A.4 and 6.9.A.1 (topic 6.1), skill 4.C. Thinking: compare the starting and final states of the two processes before reading attractions from a sign. Trap: (A), attractions judged from ΔH alone.

mc.stem:
Questions 16-18 refer to the following.

A self-heating can of coffee has an inner chamber, separated from the coffee by a thin steel wall. When a button is pressed, water stored in the chamber is released onto solid calcium oxide:
CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(s)   ΔH = −65.2 kJ/mol
The designers want to warm 210 g of coffee from 20.0 °C to 60.0 °C. Treat the coffee as water, with a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g·°C). Molar masses: CaO, 56.08 g/mol; Ca(OH)₂, 74.09 g/mol.

parts.q:
If all of the heat released went into the coffee, what is the smallest mass of CaO that the chamber must hold?
(A) 30.2 g
(B) 39.9 g
(C) 45.3 g
(D) 7.22 g
parts.a: (A). The coffee must absorb q = 210 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × 40.0 °C = 35 112 J = 35.1 kJ. Each mole of CaO releases 65.2 kJ, so 35.1 kJ ÷ 65.2 kJ/mol = 0.539 mol of CaO, and 0.539 mol × 56.08 g/mol = 30.2 g. (B) converts moles to grams with the molar mass of the product, Ca(OH)₂. (C) uses the final temperature, 60.0 °C, as if it were the temperature change. (D) leaves the specific heat capacity out of q, using 210 × 40.0 = 8400 J.
parts.n: 6.6.A.1 and 6.4.A.1 (topic 6.6), skill 5.F. Thinking: chain q = mcΔT to moles through ΔH, then to grams of the right substance. Trap: (C), the final temperature used as ΔT.

parts.q:
In a test of a prototype, 30.2 g of CaO reacts completely, but the coffee warms only from 20.0 °C to 48.0 °C. An engineer concludes that the value ΔH = −65.2 kJ/mol must be too negative. Which of the following best evaluates the engineer's conclusion?
(A) It is justified: the coffee rose only 70% as far as expected, so ΔH is about 70% of −65.2 kJ/mol
(B) It is not justified: 35.1 kJ is still released, but part of it warms the can and chamber or escapes
(C) It is justified: the Ca(OH)₂ that forms absorbs part of the heat, and that makes the true ΔH smaller
(D) It cannot be judged: ΔH values apply only at 25 °C, and the coffee ended at 48.0 °C, not 25 °C
parts.a: (B). ΔH is the heat released per mole of reaction, and 0.539 mol of CaO still releases 0.539 × 65.2 = 35.1 kJ. But the coffee is not the only thing that warms: the steel can, the Ca(OH)₂ and any leftover water in the chamber are heated too, and some energy passes to the air. The coffee received only 210 × 4.18 × 28.0 = 24.6 kJ, about 70% of the heat released. (A) assumes that every joule went into the coffee, the very assumption the test shows is false. (C) counts heat that warms the product as a change in ΔH; that heat was released by the reaction and simply ended up in the solid instead of the coffee. (D) misapplies standard conditions: ΔH changes very little between 25 °C and 48 °C, far too little to explain a 30% shortfall.
parts.n: 6.4.A.2 and 6.6.A.2 (topic 6.4), skill 6.G. Thinking: separate the energy a reaction releases from the share of it that reaches the object being measured. Trap: (A), which assumes no heat went anywhere else.

parts.q:
In a second prototype, the reaction has finished when a thermometer in the chamber reads 90 °C and one in the coffee reads 30 °C. Some minutes later both read 52 °C. Assume that during this time energy passes only from the chamber's contents to the coffee. Which of the following best accounts for these observations?
(A) At 52 °C the chamber's particles still have the greater average kinetic energy, because the chamber started out hotter.
(B) Energy flowed until the chamber and the coffee held equal total thermal energy, which happened when both reached 52 °C.
(C) Energy flowed until average kinetic energies matched; the chamber's temperature changed more because its heat capacity is smaller.
(D) Energy flowed until average kinetic energies matched; the chamber's temperature changed more because its heat capacity is greater.
parts.a: (C). Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy of the particles. The chamber's faster particles collide with the particles of the steel wall, and these collide with the slower coffee molecules, so energy passes to the coffee until the average kinetic energies, and so the temperatures, are equal at 52 °C. With no energy going anywhere else, the energy the chamber's contents lose equals the energy the coffee gains: the coffee gains 210 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × 22 °C = 19.3 kJ, while the chamber's contents cool by 38 °C, so their heat capacity is about 19.3 kJ ÷ 38 °C = 0.51 kJ/°C, against 0.88 kJ/°C for the coffee. The same energy changes the temperature of the smaller heat capacity more. (A) contradicts thermal equilibrium: equal temperatures mean equal average kinetic energies, whatever the starting temperatures. (B) sets the end point at equal total energy, but net transfer stops when the temperatures are equal; bodies with different heat capacities hold different amounts of thermal energy at the same temperature. (D) has the heat capacity backward: for the same energy, a larger heat capacity would change temperature less, not more.
parts.n: 6.3.A.2, 6.3.A.3 and 6.4.A.3 (topic 6.3), skill 6.E. Thinking: explain the common final temperature by collisions that even out average kinetic energy, then use the unequal temperature changes and energy conservation to compare heat capacities. Trap: (D), which links the larger temperature change to the larger heat capacity.

mc.stem:
Questions 19-20 refer to the following.

Dissolving an ionic solid can be pictured as two steps: first the ions of the solid are separated into gaseous ions, and then the gaseous ions are surrounded by water molecules (hydration). The table gives approximate values for three chlorides, in kJ per mole of solid.
Salt · energy needed to separate the ions · enthalpy change of hydrating the gaseous ions · ΔH_soln
LiCl · +853 · −890 · −37
NaCl · +787 · −783 · +4
KCl · +715 · −698 · +17

parts.q:
Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data?
(A) KCl dissolves endothermically because its ions are held together more strongly than the ions in LiCl
(B) The sign of ΔH_soln is set by the energy needed to separate the ions alone, the larger of the two steps
(C) LiCl dissolves exothermically because separating its ions releases more energy than hydrating them absorbs
(D) From LiCl to KCl, hydration becomes less exothermic by more than the separation energy falls
parts.a: (D). ΔH_soln is the sum of the two steps (for LiCl, +853 − 890 = −37 kJ/mol). From LiCl to KCl the energy needed to separate the ions falls by 853 − 715 = 138 kJ/mol, which on its own would make dissolving more exothermic, but the hydration enthalpy becomes less negative by 890 − 698 = 192 kJ/mol. The larger change wins, so ΔH_soln rises from −37 to +17 kJ/mol. (A) reverses the data: KCl needs the least energy, 715 kJ/mol, to separate its ions. (B) ignores the hydration step, which is as large as the separation step and, for LiCl, larger; the sign depends on the small difference between two large numbers. (C) has the energy flows backward: separating ions absorbs energy and hydrating them releases it.
parts.n: 6.9.A.1 and 6.1.A.4 (topic 6.9), skill 6.B. Thinking: add the two steps and compare how much each one changes across the series. Trap: (A), which reads the separation energy backward.

parts.q:
A student dissolves 5.0 g of KCl in 100.0 g of water in an insulated cup, and the temperature falls from 22.0 °C to 19.4 °C. Which of the following best explains the temperature drop, using the values in the table?
(A) Hydration releases 698 kJ/mol, less than the 715 kJ/mol needed to separate the ions, so the rest comes from particle motion
(B) Separating the ions absorbs 715 kJ/mol and hydrating them absorbs another 698 kJ/mol, so the water supplies energy for both steps
(C) The ion–water attractions formed are stronger than the attractions in the solid, and forming stronger attractions absorbs energy
(D) The dissolved ions spread through the water, so the same thermal energy is shared among more particles and the temperature falls
parts.a: (A). By the table, separating the ions of 1 mol of KCl absorbs 715 kJ while hydrating them releases 698 kJ, so the process needs a net 17 kJ/mol. In an insulated cup that energy can come only from the kinetic energy of the particles already there, mostly water molecules, so their average kinetic energy, and the temperature, falls. For 5.0 g (0.067 mol) that is 1.14 kJ, enough to cool 105 g of solution by about 2.6 °C. (B) has hydration absorbing energy; forming ion–dipole attractions releases energy. (C) also has forming attractions absorb energy, and stronger attractions formed would release more energy than was absorbed and warm the water. (D) treats temperature as energy shared out among particles; energy is conserved, and the water cools only because energy is used to separate the ions.
parts.n: 6.1.A.4 and 6.6.A.3 (topic 6.1), skill 4.C. Thinking: connect the net energy of the two steps to a change in the particles' kinetic energy. Trap: (D), temperature diluted among more particles.

parts.q:
A student estimates ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g) (ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH) from these average bond enthalpies, in kJ/mol: C=C 614, C−C 348, C−H 413, O−H 463, C−O 358. Her work:
Step 1. Bonds broken: 1 C=C + 4 C−H + 2 O−H = 614 + 1652 + 926 = 3192 kJ
Step 2. Bonds formed: 1 C−C + 5 C−H + 1 C−O + 1 O−H = 348 + 2065 + 358 + 463 = 3234 kJ
Step 3. ΔH = bonds formed − bonds broken = 3234 − 3192 = +42 kJ
Step 4. ΔH is positive, so the reaction is endothermic.
Which of the following correctly identifies the first error in her work?
(A) Step 1, because only one of the two O−H bonds in each water molecule actually breaks
(B) Step 2, because an ethanol molecule contains six C−H bonds, not five
(C) Step 3, because ΔH is bonds broken minus bonds formed, which gives −42 kJ
(D) Step 4, because a reaction that forms more bonds than it breaks must be exothermic
parts.a: (C). Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it, so ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = 3192 − 3234 = −42 kJ: the reaction is exothermic, because the bonds formed are stronger in total than those broken. Step 3 subtracts the wrong way round, and Step 4's conclusion follows from that error. (A) describes a different bookkeeping that gives the same answer: counting only the bonds that change (break C=C and one O−H; form C−C, one C−H and C−O) gives 614 + 463 − (348 + 413 + 358) = −42 kJ, so counting every bond in Step 1 is not an error. (B) miscounts ethanol: CH₃CH₂OH has 3 + 2 = 5 C−H bonds and one O−H bond. (D) judges by the number of bonds rather than their strengths, and in any case Step 3 is already wrong before Step 4.
parts.n: 6.7.A.2 (topic 6.7), skill 6.D. Thinking: check each step against the sign convention that breaking absorbs and forming releases. Trap: (A), which mistakes a valid full count for an error.

parts.q:
A student wants to find ΔH for CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s). This reaction is far too slow to follow in a coffee-cup calorimeter, but both CaO(s) and CaCO₃(s) react quickly and completely with excess hydrochloric acid, and CO₂(g) does not react with hydrochloric acid. Which plan would give ΔH for the target reaction?
(A) Measure ΔH for CaO(s) and for CaCO₃(s), each with excess HCl(aq), then add the two values
(B) Measure ΔH for CaO(s) and for CaCO₃(s), each with excess HCl(aq), then subtract the second from the first
(C) Measure ΔH for CaO(s) with excess HCl(aq) and for CO₂(g) bubbled into HCl(aq), then add the two
(D) Measure the heat as CaCO₃(s) is heated strongly in the calorimeter until CO₂ forms, then reverse its sign
parts.a: (B). The two measurable reactions are CaO(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l), ΔH₁, and CaCO₃(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), ΔH₂. Reversing the second and adding it to the first cancels the HCl, CaCl₂ and H₂O and leaves CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s), so ΔH = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂. (A) adds the equations without reversing one, which does not cancel the CaCl₂ and H₂O. (C) cannot work: CO₂ does not react with HCl(aq), so there is nothing to measure, and no step involves CaCO₃. (D) is not a coffee-cup measurement: decomposing CaCO₃ needs a flame far hotter than the cup can hold, and the heat supplied by the flame cannot be told apart from the heat of reaction.
parts.n: 6.9.A.1 and 6.9.B.2 (topic 6.9), skill 2.C. Thinking: choose two measurable reactions whose equations combine into the target. Trap: (A), adding without reversing.

parts.q:
A 0.500 mol sample of a solid, X, in an insulated container is heated by a 50.0 W (50.0 J/s) heater. The heating curve, temperature against time, is made of straight segments: from 0 to 60 s it rises from 20 °C to 44 °C; from 60 s to 180 s it is flat at 44 °C; from 180 s to 380 s it rises from 44 °C to 84 °C; and from 380 s to 980 s it is flat at 84 °C. Assume all of the heater's energy goes into X. Which conclusion do the data support?
(A) ΔH_vap of X is 60.0 kJ/mol, and liquid X has a larger molar heat capacity than solid X
(B) ΔH_vap of X is 60.0 kJ/mol, and solid X has a larger molar heat capacity than liquid X
(C) ΔH_vap of X is 30.0 kJ/mol, and liquid X has a larger molar heat capacity than solid X
(D) ΔH_vap of X is 15.0 kJ/mol, and solid X has a larger molar heat capacity than liquid X
parts.a: (A). The boiling plateau lasts 980 − 380 = 600 s, so X absorbs 50.0 J/s × 600 s = 30 000 J while 0.500 mol boils: ΔH_vap = 30.0 kJ ÷ 0.500 mol = 60.0 kJ/mol. For the heat capacities compare the sloped segments: the solid rises 24 °C on 3000 J, which is 3000 J ÷ 24 °C ÷ 0.500 mol = 250 J/(mol·°C); the liquid rises 40 °C on 10 000 J, which is 500 J/(mol·°C). The liquid's gentler slope means it needs more energy per degree. (B) reads the steeper slope as the larger heat capacity, but a steeper rise means fewer joules per degree. (C) forgets to divide the 30.0 kJ by 0.500 mol. (D) multiplies by 0.500 mol instead of dividing and also misreads the slopes.
parts.n: 6.5.A.1 and 6.4.A.5 (topic 6.5), skill 5.D. Thinking: read energy from time at constant power, and heat capacity from the inverse of the slope. Trap: (B), a steeper slope taken to mean a larger heat capacity.

parts.q:
A 50.0 g block of copper at 80.0 °C and a 50.0 g block of aluminum at 20.0 °C are placed in contact inside an insulated box. The specific heat capacities are 0.385 J/(g·°C) for copper and 0.897 J/(g·°C) for aluminum. Which prediction of the final temperature, with its reasoning, is correct?
(A) About 50 °C, because blocks of equal mass share the temperature change equally
(B) About 62 °C, because copper, with its lower specific heat, changes temperature less than aluminum
(C) About 38 °C, because energy flows until the two blocks contain equal amounts of thermal energy
(D) About 38 °C, because each degree aluminum warms takes more energy than each degree copper cools
parts.a: (D). The energy lost by the copper equals the energy gained by the aluminum: 50.0 × 0.385 × (80.0 − T) = 50.0 × 0.897 × (T − 20.0), so T = 38.0 °C. Aluminum needs 0.897 J per gram per degree against copper's 0.385, so the copper cools 42 °C while the aluminum warms only 18 °C. (A) would hold only if the specific heats were equal. (B) swaps the roles of the specific heats: copper's lower specific heat means its temperature changes more, not less, for the same energy. (C) gives the right temperature for the wrong reason: net transfer stops when the temperatures, the average kinetic energies of the particles, are equal; blocks with different heat capacities at the same temperature do not hold equal thermal energy.
parts.n: 6.3.A.3 and 6.4.A.3 (topic 6.3), skill 4.A. Thinking: set energy lost equal to energy gained, then see why the block with the smaller specific heat changes more. Trap: (C), the right number with the equal-energy reason.

parts.q:
To find the heat capacity of a foam-cup calorimeter, a student puts 50.0 g of water at 20.0 °C in the cup and waits until the cup is at 20.0 °C too. She then adds 50.0 g of water at 60.0 °C, stirs, and records a final temperature of 39.0 °C. Using 4.18 J/(g·°C) for water and assuming no heat is lost to the room, what is the heat capacity of the calorimeter?
(A) 418 J/°C
(B) 20.9 J/°C
(C) 22.0 J/°C
(D) 19.9 J/°C
parts.a: (C). The hot water lost 50.0 × 4.18 × (60.0 − 39.0) = 4389 J, but the cold water gained only 50.0 × 4.18 × (39.0 − 20.0) = 3971 J. The missing 418 J went into the cup, which warmed with the cold water from 20.0 °C to 39.0 °C, a change of 19.0 °C, so its heat capacity is 418 J ÷ 19.0 °C = 22.0 J/°C. (A) forgets to divide by the cup's temperature change. (B) divides by 20.0 °C, the rise the cold water would have had with no cup (40.0 − 20.0). (D) divides by 21.0 °C, the hot water's temperature change, but the cup started at the cold water's temperature.
parts.n: 6.4.A.1 and 6.4.A.2 (topic 6.4), skill 2.D. Thinking: find the heat the two water samples do not share and give it to the part of the system that absorbed it. Trap: (D), the hot water's temperature change.

fr.title: Bleach and thiosulfate: a mole ratio from temperature rises
fr.stem:
In basic solution, hypochlorite ion, OCl⁻, oxidizes thiosulfate ion, S₂O₃²⁻, to sulfate ion in a fast, exothermic reaction. To find the mole ratio in which OCl⁻ and S₂O₃²⁻ react, a student mixes different volumes of 0.200 M NaOCl(aq) and 0.200 M Na₂S₂O₃(aq) in a foam cup, always making a total of 50.0 mL, and records the largest temperature rise. The NaOCl solution also contains NaOH, so OH⁻ is always in excess. Both solutions start at 22.0 °C.
Trial · volume of NaOCl(aq) (mL) · volume of Na₂S₂O₃(aq) (mL) · largest temperature rise (°C)
1 · 10.0 · 40.0 · 2.9
2 · 20.0 · 30.0 · 5.8
3 · 25.0 · 25.0 · 7.2
4 · 30.0 · 20.0 · 8.7
5 · 35.0 · 15.0 · 10.1
6 · 40.0 · 10.0 · 11.6
7 · 45.0 · 5.0 · 5.8
Assume every mixture has a density of 1.00 g/mL and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g·°C), and that the cup absorbs no heat.

parts.q: Based on the data, determine the mole ratio of OCl⁻ to S₂O₃²⁻ in the reaction. Justify your answer by explaining why the largest temperature rise occurs in that mixture.
parts.a: 4 : 1 (1 point). The largest rise, 11.6 °C, is in trial 6, which mixes 40.0 mL × 0.200 M = 8.00 mmol OCl⁻ with 10.0 mL × 0.200 M = 2.00 mmol S₂O₃²⁻, a 4 : 1 ratio. Every mixture has the same mass, so the temperature rise is proportional to the heat released and so to the amount of reaction. When the reactants are mixed in the ratio in which they react, both are used up completely and the most reaction occurs; in every other mixture one reactant is limiting and some of the other is left over, so less reaction occurs and less heat is released (1 point).
parts.n: '4 : 1' with no link between the limiting reactant and the size of ΔT earns only the first point. 'Trial 6 has the most reactant' earns nothing: every trial holds 10.0 mmol of solute in all. Reading the ratio as 1 : 4 earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain why the student keeps the total volume at 50.0 mL in every trial.
parts.a: So that every trial heats the same mass of solution, 50.0 g. With m and c fixed, q = mcΔT makes ΔT proportional to the heat released, so the temperature rises of different trials can be compared directly as measures of how much reaction occurred. (With equal concentrations, the fixed volume also keeps the total amount of reactant at 10.0 mmol, so that only the ratio changes.)
parts.n: 'To make it a fair test' or 'to control variables', without saying that a fixed mass makes ΔT track the heat released, earns nothing.

parts.q: Using trial 6, calculate ΔH for the reaction in kilojoules per mole of S₂O₃²⁻.
parts.a: −1.21 × 10³ kJ/mol. q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × 11.6 °C = 2.42 × 10³ J released by the reaction (1 point). In trial 6 neither reactant is in excess, and n(S₂O₃²⁻) = 0.0100 L × 0.200 mol/L = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol, so ΔH = −2.42 × 10³ J ÷ 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol = −1.21 × 10⁶ J/mol = −1.21 × 10³ kJ/mol (1 point).
parts.n: Dividing by the moles of OCl⁻ (8.00 × 10⁻³ mol) gives −303 kJ per mole of OCl⁻ and does not earn the second point. A positive ΔH earns at most the first point.

parts.q: A classmate points out that no trial was run between 40.0 mL and 45.0 mL of NaOCl(aq), so the true peak could lie between trials 6 and 7, and the ratio could be 5 : 1 rather than 4 : 1. Use the results of trials 2 and 7 to evaluate the classmate's claim.
parts.a: The claim is wrong: the data rule out 5 : 1. In trial 7, S₂O₃²⁻ is limiting (1.00 mmol against 9.00 mmol of OCl⁻, and it would be for any ratio below 9 : 1), so a rise of 5.8 °C corresponds to 1.00 mmol of S₂O₃²⁻ reacting (1 point). Trial 2 also rises 5.8 °C, so 1.00 mmol of S₂O₃²⁻ reacted there too, and in trial 2 OCl⁻ is limiting at 4.00 mmol: 4.00 mol of OCl⁻ react per mole of S₂O₃²⁻. A 5 : 1 ratio would let 4.00 mmol of OCl⁻ react with only 0.80 mmol of S₂O₃²⁻, giving a rise of about 0.80 × 5.8 = 4.6 °C, not the 5.8 °C observed (1 point). (Equally: the rising points lie on a line through the origin, about 0.29 °C per mL of NaOCl, and the line from trial 7 to 0 °C at 50.0 mL falls 1.16 °C per mL; the two lines cross at 40.0 mL, a 4 : 1 ratio.)
parts.n: Agreeing with the classmate earns nothing. 'More trials are needed' without using the data earns nothing: the point is that the S₂O₃²⁻-limited trial 7 fixes the temperature rise per mole of reaction.

parts.q: The student's cup had no lid, so in every trial some heat escaped to the room before the largest temperature was reached. Predict the effect of this on (i) the magnitude of ΔH calculated in part (c) and (ii) the mole ratio found in part (a). Justify each prediction.
parts.a: (i) Too small (1 point): heat that escapes does not show up as a temperature rise, so the measured ΔT and the calculated q are smaller than the heat actually released, and |ΔH| comes out smaller than the true value. (ii) Unaffected (1 point): every trial loses a similar fraction of its heat, so every rise is lowered by about the same factor, and the largest rise still occurs in the same mixture, 40.0 mL to 10.0 mL; the ratio depends on where the peak is, not on how high it is.
parts.n: 'ΔH too large, because heat was lost' earns nothing for (i). 'The ratio changes, because the temperatures are wrong' earns nothing for (ii). A prediction without a reason earns nothing.

parts.q: Predict the largest temperature rise if trial 6 were repeated with 0.400 M solutions of both reactants. Justify your prediction.
parts.a: About 23 °C, twice 11.6 °C. Doubling both concentrations doubles the moles of each reactant in the same 50.0 mL, still in the 4 : 1 ratio, so twice as much reaction occurs and twice the heat is released into the same mass of solution: ΔT ≈ 2 × 11.6 = 23.2 °C (a little less in practice, since a hotter cup loses heat faster).
parts.n: '11.6 °C, because ΔH per mole does not change' earns nothing: ΔH per mole is unchanged, but twice as many moles react in the same mass of solution.

fr.title: Ozone and oxygen atoms: formation and bond enthalpies
fr.stem:
High in the atmosphere, oxygen atoms react with ozone: O₃(g) + O(g) → 2 O₂(g). In an O₃ molecule the central O atom is joined to each of the other two O atoms by an identical bond.
Species · ΔH°f (kJ/mol)
O₃(g) · +142.7
O(g) · +249.2
O₂(g) · 0
Average bond enthalpies: O=O (in O₂), 498 kJ/mol; O−O single bond (as in H₂O₂), 146 kJ/mol.

parts.q: Calculate ΔH° for the reaction.
parts.a: ΔH° = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants) = 2(0) − (142.7 + 249.2) = −391.9 kJ per mole of reaction.
parts.n: +391.9 kJ (reactants minus products) earns nothing.

parts.q: Use your answer to part (a) and the O=O bond enthalpy to estimate the average enthalpy of one of the oxygen–oxygen bonds in O₃.
parts.a: About 302 kJ/mol. The reaction breaks the two oxygen–oxygen bonds in O₃ (the O atom has no bonds) and forms two O=O bonds: ΔH = 2x − 2(498) = −391.9 kJ, so 2x = 604 kJ and x = 302 kJ/mol.
parts.n: Treating O₃ as having a single bond to break (x = 604 kJ/mol), or subtracting 498 kJ for the O atom, earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain why the bond enthalpy found in part (b) lies between the O−O single-bond enthalpy and the O=O double-bond enthalpy.
parts.a: O₃ has two resonance structures, each with one single and one double bond, and the real molecule is an average of the two: both bonds are identical, with a bond order of 1.5. A bond between a single and a double bond in order is stronger than an O−O single bond (146 kJ/mol) and weaker than an O=O double bond (498 kJ/mol).
parts.n: 'Because O₃ has one single and one double bond' earns nothing: the two bonds are identical, which is exactly what resonance explains.

parts.q: A student argues that because the ΔH°f values of both O₃(g) and O(g) are positive, making them requires energy, so the reaction between them must absorb energy too. Evaluate the student's argument.
parts.a: The argument is wrong. A positive ΔH°f means only that each reactant is higher in enthalpy than O₂(g), the element in its standard state. The reaction turns both into O₂(g), with ΔH°f = 0, so the products are lower in enthalpy than the reactants and the reaction releases the 391.9 kJ found in part (a), the energy that was stored when O and O₃ were made from O₂. In bond terms, the two O=O bonds formed (996 kJ) are stronger than the two bonds broken in O₃ (604 kJ).
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'Disagree, ΔH is negative' with no reason tied to the enthalpies of formation or to bond strengths earns nothing.

fr.title: Boiling ethanol at two heater powers
fr.stem:
To measure the molar enthalpy of vaporization of ethanol, C₂H₅OH (46.07 g/mol), at its boiling point, a student places an electric immersion heater in ethanol that is already boiling steadily at 78 °C in an open flask on a balance. She records the mass of ethanol lost per minute at two heater powers. The flask and its contents stay at 78 °C in both runs, and the room is at 22 °C.
Run · heater power (J/s) · mass of ethanol lost per minute (g/min)
1 · 30.0 · 1.79
2 · 50.0 · 3.22
The accepted value of ΔH_vap of ethanol at its boiling point is 38.6 kJ/mol.

parts.q: Using run 1 alone, and assuming that all of the heater's energy vaporizes ethanol, calculate ΔH_vap.
parts.a: 46.3 kJ/mol. In one minute the heater supplies 30.0 J/s × 60 s = 1800 J, and 1.79 g ÷ 46.07 g/mol = 0.0389 mol of ethanol vaporizes, so ΔH_vap = 1800 J ÷ 0.0389 mol = 4.63 × 10⁴ J/mol = 46.3 kJ/mol.
parts.n: An answer per gram (1.01 kJ/g) with no conversion to moles, or one that leaves out the 60 s in a minute (0.772 kJ/mol), earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain why the value from part (a) is greater than the accepted value.
parts.a: The flask at 78 °C is hotter than the room at 22 °C, so some of the heater's energy leaves the flask as heat to the surroundings instead of vaporizing ethanol. The calculation credits all 1800 J to the 1.79 g that vaporized, so it overstates the energy needed per mole.
parts.n: 'Human error', or 'heat was lost' without saying that the lost energy was counted as energy of vaporization, earns nothing.

parts.q: The student reasons that, because the flask stays at 78 °C in both runs, heat escapes to the room at the same rate in both. Using this assumption and both runs, calculate ΔH_vap, and explain why this method removes the effect of the heat loss.
parts.a: 38.7 kJ/mol. The heat lost per minute is the same in both runs, so it cancels in the difference between them: the extra (50.0 − 30.0) J/s × 60 s = 1200 J per minute in run 2 all goes into vaporizing the extra 3.22 − 1.79 = 1.43 g (0.0310 mol) per minute, so ΔH_vap = 1200 J ÷ 0.0310 mol = 3.87 × 10⁴ J/mol = 38.7 kJ/mol, close to the accepted value.
parts.n: Averaging the two single-run values ((46.3 + 42.9) ÷ 2 = 44.6 kJ/mol) earns nothing: each of them still includes the heat loss.

parts.q: Another student says that because the temperature of the ethanol does not rise while the heater is on, the ethanol is not gaining any energy, so all of the heater's energy must be escaping to the room. Evaluate this claim.
parts.a: The claim is wrong. At the boiling point the energy absorbed goes into overcoming the attractions (hydrogen bonds and dispersion forces) between ethanol molecules as the liquid becomes gas. It raises the potential energy of the molecules, not their average kinetic energy, so the temperature stays at 78 °C. The balance shows ethanol leaving as vapor, and the rate of loss rises with the heater power, which could not happen if all of the energy escaped.
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'Disagree, energy is conserved' without saying where the energy goes (into separating molecules at constant temperature) earns nothing.

u7.intro: A periodic table and the AP Chemistry equations sheet are allowed, and a calculator may be used throughout.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-3 refer to the following.

A student studies the equilibrium below. Both cobalt species are dissolved, and water is the solvent.
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + 4 Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq) + 6 H₂O(l)
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pink and [CoCl₄]²⁻ is blue; a solution containing a mixture of both looks violet. The student puts 5 mL of a violet stock solution in each of six test tubes, treats each tube as shown, and records the color once no further change occurs.
Tube · treatment · final color
1 · none (reference) · violet
2 · 1 mL of 12 M HCl added · blue
3 · 5 mL of distilled water added · pink
4 · 5 drops of 0.1 M AgNO₃ added; a white precipitate forms · pink
5 · placed in an 80 °C water bath · blue
6 · placed in an ice-water bath · pink

parts.q:
Which conclusion about the forward reaction is best supported by tubes 5 and 6?
(A) It is endothermic, because a higher temperature increases K and shifts the system toward [CoCl₄]²⁻.
(B) It is exothermic, because the heat released as [CoCl₄]²⁻ forms is what turns the heated tube blue.
(C) It is endothermic, because heating speeds up the forward reaction but does not speed up the reverse.
(D) It is exothermic, because cooling slows both reactions, so the pink ion is left over in the cold tube.
parts.a: (A). Heating turns the solution blue and cooling turns it pink, so a higher temperature favors [CoCl₄]²⁻. Only a change in temperature changes K, and K increases with temperature for an endothermic reaction: the system absorbs the added heat by shifting toward products. (B) reverses the logic: if forming [CoCl₄]²⁻ released heat, adding heat would push the system toward the pink ion. (C) has the right sign for the wrong reason: heating speeds up both the forward and the reverse reactions; what matters is that it changes their ratio at equilibrium, which is K. (D) confuses how fast equilibrium is reached with where it lies; slower rates in the ice bath do not decide which color the tube ends up.
parts.n: 7.9.A.1 and 7.9.A.2 (topic 7.9), skill 6.F. Thinking: read the direction of a temperature shift from the colors, then connect a K that rises with temperature to an endothermic forward reaction. Trap: (C), the right sign justified by a rate argument.

parts.q:
To explain tube 3, a student writes: 'Water is a product of the forward reaction. Adding water increases the concentration of a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the left.' Which of the following best evaluates the student's explanation?
(A) It is correct: adding any product makes Q greater than K, so the net reaction then runs in reverse.
(B) The shift is right but the reason is not: H₂O(l) is not in Q, and diluting the ions makes Q greater than K.
(C) It is incorrect: dilution lowers every ion concentration by the same factor, so Q stays equal to K throughout.
(D) The reason is right but the evidence is weak: tube 3 could look pink simply because it is more dilute.
parts.a: (B). Water is the solvent, a pure liquid whose concentration hardly changes, so it does not appear in Q = [CoCl₄]²⁻ / ([Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺[Cl⁻]⁴). Doubling the volume halves every ion concentration, and because the denominator holds five factors of concentration and the numerator one, Q becomes 2⁴ = 16 times larger than K. Net reverse reaction follows and the tube turns pink. (A) repeats the student's error: H₂O(l) is not in the expression, so adding it cannot change Q by acting as a product. (C) assumes dilution cannot change Q; that is true only when both sides have the same number of dissolved particles. (D) forgets that dilution alone would make violet paler, not change it to pink; a change of hue means the ratio of the two cobalt ions changed.
parts.n: 7.3.A.2 and 7.10.A.1 (topic 7.10), skill 6.D. Thinking: separate a correct prediction from a correct justification by writing Q and asking what dilution does to it. Trap: (A), because 'water is a product' sounds like Le Chatelier's principle.

parts.q:
A classmate suggests that tube 5 turned blue only because water evaporated from the hot tube, which raised [Cl⁻], and not because of the temperature itself. Which additional observation would best rule out the classmate's explanation?
(A) A tube held in a 90 °C bath turns blue faster than a tube held in the 80 °C bath.
(B) Adding 1 mL of 12 M HCl to tube 5 while it is still hot makes it a deeper blue.
(C) A tube of distilled water left in the 80 °C bath for the same time loses some mass.
(D) A stoppered tube turns blue at 80 °C and turns violet again when it cools to 22 °C.
parts.a: (D). A stopper prevents evaporation, so a stoppered tube that still turns blue rules out a higher [Cl⁻] as the cause; and a color change that reverses on cooling, with no water returned to the solution, can only come from the temperature changing the position of the equilibrium. (A) shows that the color changes faster at higher temperature, a statement about rate, which evaporation would also explain. (B) shows that extra Cl⁻ turns the solution bluer, which is the classmate's mechanism, not evidence against it. (C) shows that water does evaporate in the bath, which supports the classmate rather than ruling the idea out.
parts.n: 7.9.A.1 (topic 7.9), skill 2.C. Thinking: choose the control that removes one variable (evaporation) while keeping the other (temperature). Trap: (C), a measurement about evaporation that supports the rival explanation.

mc.stem:
Questions 4-6 refer to the following.

Compound X converts to its isomer Y in the gas phase: X(g) ⇌ Y(g). Both the forward and the reverse reactions are elementary, so the forward rate = k₁[X] and the reverse rate = k₂[Y]. A rigid flask at constant temperature initially contains 0.1000 M X and no Y. The table gives [X] and the rates of the two reactions at several times.
Time (s) · [X] (M) · forward rate (M/s) · reverse rate (M/s)
0 · 0.1000 · 3.00 × 10⁻³ · 0
20 · 0.0587 · 1.76 × 10⁻³ · 4.13 × 10⁻⁴
40 · 0.0401 · 1.20 × 10⁻³ · 5.99 × 10⁻⁴
80 · 0.0281 · 8.42 × 10⁻⁴ · 7.19 × 10⁻⁴
150 · 0.0252 · 7.56 × 10⁻⁴ · 7.48 × 10⁻⁴
300 · 0.0250 · 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ · 7.50 × 10⁻⁴
400 · 0.0250 · 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ · 7.50 × 10⁻⁴

parts.q:
Which statement correctly describes the mixture at t = 40 s?
(A) Q > K, since [Y] is already greater than [X], so there is a net conversion of Y into X.
(B) Q < K, since the forward rate is greater than the reverse rate, so there is a net conversion of X into Y.
(C) Q = K, since the forward and reverse reactions are both occurring, so there is no net change at all.
(D) Q < K, since [X] is still falling, so the forward reaction is occurring but the reverse has not yet begun.
parts.a: (B). At 40 s the forward rate (1.20 × 10⁻³ M/s) exceeds the reverse rate (5.99 × 10⁻⁴ M/s), so X is converted into Y faster than Y reverts; [X] keeps falling until 300 s. Numerically, [Y] = 0.1000 − 0.0401 = 0.0599 M, so Q = 0.0599 ÷ 0.0401 = 1.49, while K = 0.0750 ÷ 0.0250 = 3.0 from the equilibrium rows. (A) compares Q with 1 instead of with K: [Y] > [X] at 40 s, but Q is still below K. (C) treats 'both reactions are happening' as equilibrium; they happen from the moment Y appears, and equilibrium needs their rates to be equal. (D) gets Q < K right but ignores the reverse-rate column, which is already 5.99 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
parts.n: 7.2.A.1 and 7.7.A.2 (topic 7.2), skill 5.D. Thinking: read the direction of net change from the relative rates and check it against Q and K. Trap: (A), comparing Q with 1 rather than with K.

parts.q:
A student notes that [X] changes by less than 1% between t = 150 s and t = 300 s, and concludes that the mixture was already at equilibrium at t = 150 s. Which of the following best evaluates the conclusion?
(A) It is not supported: at 150 s the forward rate, 7.56 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, still exceeds the reverse rate, so X is still turning into Y.
(B) It is supported: at 150 s both the forward and the reverse reactions are occurring, and that is what defines a system at equilibrium.
(C) It is supported: [X] changes by less than 1% after 150 s, which shows that the forward and reverse rates are equal from that time on.
(D) It is not supported: at equilibrium both rates must fall to zero, and at 150 s both rates in the table are still well above zero.
parts.a: (A). Equilibrium requires equal forward and reverse rates. At 150 s the forward rate is 7.56 × 10⁻⁴ M/s and the reverse rate 7.48 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, so X still turns into Y a little faster than Y turns back, and [X] does fall further, from 0.0252 to 0.0250 M. Equivalently, Q = 0.0748 ÷ 0.0252 = 2.97, still below K = 0.0750 ÷ 0.0250 = 3.00; the two rates become equal only by 300 s. (B) takes 'both reactions occur' as the test for equilibrium; both have occurred since Y first formed, including at 20 s, far from equilibrium. (C) reads a small change as no change; the rate columns show that the two rates still differ at 150 s. (D) treats equilibrium as a stop; at 300 s and 400 s, when [X] no longer changes, both rates are still 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
parts.n: 7.1.A.2 and 7.1.A.3 (topic 7.1), skill 6.B. Thinking: test for equilibrium with the rate data (equal rates, Q = K), not with how small a change in concentration looks. Trap: (C), reading a small change in [X] as no change.

parts.q:
The experiment is repeated at the same temperature, but the flask initially contains 0.1000 M Y and no X. What are the initial rate of the reverse reaction and the value of [X] once equilibrium is reached?
(A) 3.00 × 10⁻³ M/s; [X] = 0.0250 M
(B) 3.00 × 10⁻³ M/s; [X] = 0.0750 M
(C) 1.00 × 10⁻³ M/s; [X] = 0.0250 M
(D) 1.00 × 10⁻³ M/s; [X] = 0.0750 M
parts.a: (C). At equilibrium k₂[Y] = 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ M/s with [Y] = 0.1000 − 0.0250 = 0.0750 M, so k₂ = 0.0100 s⁻¹, and the initial reverse rate is 0.0100 s⁻¹ × 0.1000 M = 1.00 × 10⁻³ M/s. K = 0.0750 ÷ 0.0250 = 3.0 is the same whichever side the system starts from, and the total is still 0.1000 M, so equilibrium again has [Y] = 3[X]: [X] = 0.0250 M. (A) assumes the reverse reaction starts as fast as the forward one did, which would need k₂ = k₁. (D) expects a mirror-image equilibrium with [X] = 0.0750 M, as though the final state depended on the starting side. (B) makes both of these errors.
parts.n: 7.4.A.1 and 7.2.A.1 (topic 7.4), skill 5.F. Thinking: get k₂ and K from the equilibrium rows, then see that the same equilibrium is reached from either direction. Trap: (D), the mirror-image equilibrium.

mc.stem:
Questions 7-10 refer to the following.

Hydrogen sulfide decomposes at high temperature:
2 H₂S(g) ⇌ 2 H₂(g) + S₂(g)
A student seals three different gas mixtures in rigid 1.00 L flasks, holds all three at the same temperature until no further change occurs, and then measures the concentrations.
Trial · [H₂S] (M) · [H₂] (M) · [S₂] (M)
1 · 0.100 · 0.0200 · 0.0100
2 · 0.200 · 0.0200 · 0.0400
3 · 0.0500 · 0.0400 · 0.000625

parts.q:
For each trial the student calculates [H₂][S₂]/[H₂S] and obtains 2.0 × 10⁻³, 4.0 × 10⁻³ and 5.0 × 10⁻⁴. She concludes that the three flasks cannot all have been at equilibrium at the same temperature. Which of the following best evaluates her conclusion?
(A) It is justified: an equilibrium constant must have one value at a given temperature, and her values differ eightfold.
(B) It is not justified: K depends on the starting amounts, so different trials are expected to give different values.
(C) It is not justified: values that agree within one order of magnitude are consistent with normal experimental error.
(D) It is not justified: her expression leaves out the coefficients; [H₂]²[S₂]/[H₂S]² equals 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ in all three.
parts.a: (D). The law of mass action raises each concentration to the power of its coefficient: K = [H₂]²[S₂]/[H₂S]². Trial 1 gives (0.0200)²(0.0100)/(0.100)² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, trial 2 gives (0.0200)²(0.0400)/(0.200)² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ and trial 3 gives (0.0400)²(0.000625)/(0.0500)² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, so the data are exactly what three equilibrium mixtures at one temperature should give. (A) is right that K is fixed at a given temperature but tests the wrong expression. (B) is a misconception: the equilibrium concentrations depend on the starting amounts, but K does not. (C) excuses an eightfold spread as error, when the correct expression shows no spread at all.
parts.n: 7.3.A.1 and 7.4.A.1 (topic 7.3), skill 6.B. Thinking: test a proposed expression against data from several trials, and let a constant value identify the right one. Trap: (A), which accepts the student's expression.

parts.q:
Another flask at the same temperature is filled with 0.100 M H₂S, 0.010 M H₂ and 0.010 M S₂. Which of the following correctly predicts what happens as this mixture approaches equilibrium?
(A) Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴, which is less than K, so [S₂] increases.
(B) Q = 1.0 × 10⁻³, which is greater than K, so [S₂] decreases.
(C) Q = 1.0 × 10⁴, which is greater than K, so [S₂] decreases.
(D) Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴, which is less than K, so [S₂] decreases.
parts.a: (A). With K = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ from the table, Q = (0.010)²(0.010)/(0.100)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. Q < K, so there is net forward reaction: H₂S decomposes, and [H₂] and [S₂] increase until Q rises to K. (B) leaves out the exponents, (0.010)(0.010)/0.100 = 1.0 × 10⁻³, which lands on the wrong side of K. (C) inverts the quotient, putting reactants over products. (D) finds the right Q but runs the rule backwards: Q < K means too little product, so the reaction goes forward.
parts.n: 7.7.A.2 and 7.3.A.1 (topic 7.7), skill 5.F. Thinking: build Q with the right exponents and let Q against K decide the direction. Trap: (B), the quotient without exponents.

parts.q:
In a new flask at the same temperature, the student starts with 0.100 M H₂S and nothing else. Her work: 'Let [S₂] = x at equilibrium, so [H₂] = 2x and [H₂S] = 0.100 − 2x. Because K is small, 0.100 − 2x ≈ 0.100. Then (2x)²(x)/(0.100)² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, so 4x³ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ and x = 0.0100 M.' Which of the following best evaluates her answer for [S₂]?
(A) It is correct: K is less than 10⁻³, so the simplifying assumption is valid for any starting amount of H₂S used.
(B) It is too small: her assumption ignores the H₂S that decomposes, so the true [S₂] is greater than 0.0100 M.
(C) It is too large: 2x is 20% of 0.100 M, so the assumption fails; with less H₂S left, the true [S₂] is smaller.
(D) It is too large by a factor of 2: [H₂] should equal x, not 2x, because H₂ and S₂ are both products.
parts.a: (C). Her answer means 2x = 0.0200 M of H₂S decomposed, which is 20% of 0.100 M, far more than the few percent the assumption can tolerate. The true [H₂S] is less than 0.100 M, so the right-hand side of 4x³ = K[H₂S]² is smaller than she used and x must be smaller: solving 4x³ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ (0.100 − 2x)² gives x = 0.0088 M. (A) judges the assumption by K alone; whether x is negligible depends on K and on the starting concentration together. (B) has the direction backwards: less H₂S remaining means less product at equilibrium, not more. (D) misreads the stoichiometry: 2 mol of H₂ form for every 1 mol of S₂.
parts.n: 7.7.A.1 (topic 7.7), skill 6.D. Thinking: check a simplifying assumption against its own result, then reason about which way the error goes. Trap: (A), 'K is small, so the assumption holds'.

parts.q:
A student argues: 'K for this reaction is only 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, far less than 1. So when H₂S at any concentration is sealed in a flask at this temperature, essentially none of it decomposes.' Which of the following best evaluates the argument?
(A) It is supported: a K much less than 1 means that the reactant is strongly favored whatever its concentration.
(B) It is not supported: when 0.100 M H₂S is sealed alone, about 18% of it has decomposed at equilibrium.
(C) It is not supported: a K less than 1 means that products are favored whenever the reaction starts from pure reactant.
(D) It is not supported: K fixes the fraction of H₂S that decomposes, and at every concentration that fraction is 18%.
parts.a: (B). Solving the equilibrium exactly for 0.100 M H₂S gives [S₂] = 0.0088 M and [H₂] = 0.0176 M, so about 18% of the H₂S decomposes; at 0.0100 M H₂S about 33% does. A K of 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ is small, but the extent of reaction also depends on the concentrations and on the form of the expression, and here the product side carries three powers of concentration against two. Only a K that is very small in this context, many powers of ten below the concentration terms, means the reaction barely proceeds. (A) treats every K below 1 as 'barely proceeds'. (C) inverts what K < 1 implies. (D) reaches the right verdict with a false reason: K fixes the ratio in the expression, not the fraction decomposed, which grows from 18% to 33% as [H₂S] falls from 0.100 M to 0.0100 M.
parts.n: 7.5.A.1 and 7.7.A.1 (topic 7.5), skill 6.D. Thinking: test a 'K is small, so nothing happens' claim with an actual equilibrium calculation. Trap: (A), which reads any K below 1 as negligible reaction.

mc.stem:
Questions 11-13 refer to the following.

Hydrogen is made industrially from methane and steam. The process is often described by two reactions, whose equilibrium constants (Kp) at a certain temperature are given below. All species are gases at this temperature.
Reaction 1: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3 H₂(g)   K₁ = 26
Reaction 2: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g)   K₂ = 1.4

parts.q:
A related process, dry reforming, uses carbon dioxide in place of steam:
CH₄(g) + CO₂(g) ⇌ 2 CO(g) + 2 H₂(g)
What is the equilibrium constant for dry reforming at the same temperature?
(A) 36
(B) 0.054
(C) 25
(D) 19
parts.a: (D). Dry reforming is reaction 1 plus the reverse of reaction 2: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3 H₂, then CO₂ + H₂ → CO + H₂O. Adding them cancels one H₂O and one H₂ and gives CH₄ + CO₂ ⇌ 2 CO + 2 H₂. Reversing reaction 2 inverts K₂, and adding reactions multiplies their constants: K = K₁ × (1/K₂) = 26 ÷ 1.4 = 19. (A) multiplies K₁ by K₂ without reversing reaction 2, which would put CO₂ on the product side. (B) reverses reaction 1 instead, giving K₂/K₁. (C) subtracts K₂ from K₁, treating equilibrium constants the way Hess's law treats enthalpies.
parts.n: 7.6.A.1 and 7.6.A.3 (topic 7.6), skill 5.F. Thinking: find the combination of given reactions that builds an unfamiliar industrial reaction, then apply the matching operations to K. Trap: (C), combining K values as if they were ΔH values.

parts.q:
A student finds K for ½ CO₂(g) + 2 H₂(g) ⇌ ½ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) as follows.
Step 1: Reverse reaction 1: CO + 3 H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + H₂O; K = 1/26 = 0.0385.
Step 2: Reverse reaction 2: CO₂ + H₂ ⇌ CO + H₂O; K = 1/1.4 = 0.714.
Step 3: Add them: CO₂ + 4 H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + 2 H₂O; K = 0.0385 × 0.714 = 0.0275.
Step 4: Halve every coefficient: K = 0.0275 ÷ 2 = 0.0137.
Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) Steps 1 to 3 are correct, but step 4 should take the square root of 0.0275, giving K = 0.17.
(B) Step 3 should add the two constants, giving 0.753, so step 4 then gives K = 0.753 ÷ 2 = 0.38.
(C) Steps 1 and 2 should not invert K, since reversing a reaction keeps K; the result is √(26 × 1.4) = 6.0.
(D) All four steps are correct, because halving every coefficient in an equation halves its K as well.
parts.a: (A). Reversing each reaction inverts its K (steps 1 and 2), and adding the reversed reactions multiplies the constants (step 3), giving 0.0275 for CO₂ + 4 H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + 2 H₂O. Multiplying every coefficient by ½ raises K to the power ½, because each concentration term in the expression is raised to the new, halved coefficient: K = (0.0275)^½ = 0.17. (B) replaces the correct multiplication with addition, and keeps the halving error. (C) denies that reversing a reaction changes K, but the reverse expression is the reciprocal of the forward one. (D) accepts the error in step 4: coefficients are exponents in K, so scaling them scales the exponent, not the value.
parts.n: 7.6.A.1, 7.6.A.2 and 7.6.A.3 (topic 7.6), skill 5.F. Thinking: audit each step of a K manipulation and find the operation that was applied to the value instead of to the exponent. Trap: (D), 'half the reaction, half the K'.

parts.q:
At the same temperature, a reactor contains CH₄ at 0.20 atm, H₂O at 2.0 atm, CO₂ at 1.5 atm and H₂ at 2.0 atm. Treat the overall process CH₄(g) + 2 H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + 4 H₂(g) as a single equilibrium. Which of the following is correct?
(A) Q = 30 and K = 27; because Q > K, the overall reaction proceeds in reverse.
(B) Q = 60 and K = 36; because Q > K, the overall reaction proceeds in reverse.
(C) Q = 30 and K = 36; because Q < K, the overall reaction proceeds forward.
(D) Q = 30 and K = 26; because Q > K, the overall reaction proceeds in reverse.
parts.a: (C). The overall reaction is reaction 1 plus reaction 2, so K = K₁K₂ = 26 × 1.4 = 36. Q = P(CO₂)P(H₂)⁴ / (P(CH₄)P(H₂O)²) = (1.5)(2.0)⁴ ÷ [(0.20)(2.0)²] = 24 ÷ 0.80 = 30. Q < K, so the overall reaction proceeds forward, making more CO₂ and H₂. (A) adds the constants, K₁ + K₂ = 27, which puts K on the wrong side of Q. (B) leaves the exponent 2 off P(H₂O), giving Q = 24 ÷ 0.40 = 60. (D) uses K₁ alone, as though the overall reaction were the first step.
parts.n: 7.6.A.3 and 7.10.A.1 (topic 7.6), skill 5.F. Thinking: combine two constants into the overall K, then compare it with a Q built from the overall equation. Trap: (A), adding the constants.

mc.stem:
Questions 14-16 refer to the following.

The diatomic gas X₂ dissociates into atoms: X₂(g) ⇌ 2 X(g). Two particle diagrams show the same sample in the same rigid 1.00 L vessel at equilibrium at two different temperatures. Each particle drawn represents 0.010 mol.
Diagram 1, at temperature T₁: 6 X₂ molecules and 4 X atoms.
Diagram 2, at temperature T₂: 3 X₂ molecules and 10 X atoms.
Temperature T₂ is higher than T₁.

parts.q:
What is the value of Kc at T₂, and what do the two diagrams show about the dissociation reaction?
(A) Kc = 3.3, and the dissociation is endothermic.
(B) Kc = 0.33, and the dissociation is endothermic.
(C) Kc = 0.33, and the dissociation is exothermic.
(D) Kc = 33.3, and the dissociation is endothermic.
parts.a: (B). At T₂, [X] = 10 × 0.010 mol ÷ 1.00 L = 0.10 M and [X₂] = 0.030 M, so Kc = [X]²/[X₂] = (0.10)² ÷ 0.030 = 0.33. At T₁, Kc = (0.040)² ÷ 0.060 = 0.027. K is larger at the higher temperature, so raising the temperature favors dissociation, and the forward reaction is endothermic, as breaking a bond should be. (A) leaves out the square on [X]. (C) computes K correctly but reads a K that grows with temperature as an exothermic reaction. (D) uses the particle counts as concentrations; the 0.010 mol-per-particle factor cancels only when the moles of gas do not change, and here one X₂ gives two X.
parts.n: 7.8.A.1 and 7.9.A.1 (topic 7.8), skill 5.F. Thinking: turn particle counts into concentrations, compare K at two temperatures and infer the sign of ΔH. Trap: (D), plugging in particle counts.

parts.q:
A student draws four more diagrams of the same 1.00 L vessel at T₁, with each particle again representing 0.010 mol. Which diagram could represent an equilibrium mixture at T₁?
(A) 12 X₂ molecules and 8 X atoms
(B) 10 X₂ molecules and 4 X atoms
(C) 3 X₂ molecules and 2 X atoms
(D) 24 X₂ molecules and 8 X atoms
parts.a: (D). At T₁, Kc = (0.040)² ÷ 0.060 = 0.0267. For 24 X₂ and 8 X, Q = (0.080)² ÷ 0.240 = 0.0267, which equals K. (A) keeps the 3 : 2 ratio of diagram 1, but doubling both amounts doubles Q to 0.0533; equal proportions do not mean equal Q when the exponents differ. (B) is diagram 1 with 4 more X₂ added, before the system has responded: Q = (0.040)² ÷ 0.100 = 0.016, less than K. (C) halves diagram 1, and Q = (0.020)² ÷ 0.030 = 0.0133.
parts.n: 7.8.A.1 and 7.4.A.1 (topic 7.8), skill 1.A. Thinking: test each particle diagram against K instead of against the proportions of the first diagram. Trap: (A), the same 3 : 2 ratio.

parts.q:
The Diagram 2 mixture is transferred to a 2.00 L vessel and held at T₂. Which of the following correctly predicts the result once equilibrium is re-established?
(A) More X atoms than in Diagram 2, because a larger volume increases the value of K.
(B) The same number of X atoms, because the expansion lowers both concentrations by the same factor.
(C) More X atoms than in Diagram 2, because halving each concentration makes Q half of K.
(D) Fewer X atoms than in Diagram 2, because a lower pressure favors the side with fewer gas particles.
parts.a: (C). Right after the expansion, [X] = 0.050 M and [X₂] = 0.015 M, so Q = (0.050)² ÷ 0.015 = 0.17, half of K = 0.33. Because [X] is squared in Q, halving every concentration halves Q. Q < K, so more X₂ dissociates, and the number of X atoms rises above 10. (A) has the right outcome but the wrong reason: at constant temperature K does not change. (B) forgets that the squared term makes Q respond more strongly than a single term. (D) has Le Chatelier's rule backwards: a lower pressure favors the side with more gas particles, here 2 X.
parts.n: 7.9.A.1 and 7.10.A.2 (topic 7.9), skill 6.D. Thinking: predict a volume change through Q, and keep the prediction and its reason both right. Trap: (A), the right result blamed on a change in K.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-20 refer to the following.

A student determines the Ksp of a slightly soluble salt, MX₂ (molar mass 250.0 g/mol), which dissolves as
MX₂(s) ⇌ M²⁺(aq) + 2 X⁻(aq)
Procedure: (1) Stir excess solid MX₂ with distilled water at 25 °C for one hour. (2) Filter off the undissolved solid. (3) Pipet 100.0 mL of the clear filtrate into a dry, weighed evaporating dish. (4) Evaporate the water, then heat the dish and residue to constant mass.
Measurement · mass (g)
empty evaporating dish · 38.4172
dish and dry residue · 38.4672

parts.q:
What value of Ksp for MX₂ do the student's data give?
(A) 3.2 × 10⁻⁸
(B) 8.0 × 10⁻⁹
(C) 4.0 × 10⁻⁶
(D) 8.0 × 10⁻⁶
parts.a: (A). The residue is 38.4672 − 38.4172 = 0.0500 g, or 0.0500 ÷ 250.0 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol of MX₂ in 0.1000 L, so the molar solubility is s = 2.00 × 10⁻³ M. In the saturated solution [M²⁺] = s and [X⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ = 4(2.00 × 10⁻³)³ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁸. (B) writes Ksp = s × s², dropping the factor of 2 in [X⁻]. (C) treats the salt as if it had a 1 : 1 formula, Ksp = s². (D) uses [X⁻] = 2s but forgets to square it: s × 2s = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶.
parts.n: 7.11.A.4 (topic 7.11), skill 5.F. Thinking: go from a mass of residue to a molar solubility and then to Ksp through the salt's formula. Trap: (C), the 1 : 1 expression s².

parts.q:
Suppose the student had not heated the residue to constant mass in step 4, so that it still held some water when it was weighed. How would this affect the calculated value of Ksp?
(A) It would be too low, because the water left in the residue dilutes the ions that were weighed.
(B) It would be too high, because the residue mass, and so the calculated solubility, would be too large.
(C) It would be unaffected, because water is a pure liquid and does not appear in the Ksp expression.
(D) It would be too high, because the water left in the dish would dissolve more MX₂ before the weighing.
parts.a: (B). Retained water adds to the measured mass, so the student would think more than 0.0500 g of MX₂ had dissolved in 100.0 mL. A larger s gives a larger Ksp, and since Ksp = 4s³, the error in s is magnified about threefold in Ksp. (A) gets the direction wrong: the weighed residue is not a solution, and extra mass can only raise the calculated s. (C) applies a true rule about the Ksp expression to a weighing error, which it does not govern. (D) has the right direction but a wrong reason: no further MX₂ enters the residue, since only the MX₂ dissolved in the 100.0 mL of filtrate is there.
parts.n: 7.11.A.4 (topic 7.11), skill 6.G. Thinking: trace a mass error through s to Ksp. Trap: (C), which applies 'pure liquids are left out of K' to a measurement error.

parts.q:
Using the value of Ksp from the student's data, what would the molar solubility of MX₂ have been if the student had stirred the solid with 0.050 M M(NO₃)₂(aq) instead of distilled water in step 1?
(A) 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ M
(B) 2.0 × 10⁻³ M
(C) 6.4 × 10⁻⁷ M
(D) 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ M
parts.a: (D). With [M²⁺] = 0.050 + s ≈ 0.050 M and [X⁻] = 2s, Ksp = (0.050)(2s)² = 0.20 s² = 3.2 × 10⁻⁸, so s² = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ and s = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ M, five times smaller than in water; s is less than 1% of 0.050, so the approximation holds. (A) writes [X⁻] as s instead of 2s: 0.050 s² = 3.2 × 10⁻⁸ gives 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. (B) assumes that a fixed Ksp means a fixed solubility, ignoring the common ion. (C) divides Ksp by 0.050 and stops, as though Ksp were [M²⁺] × s.
parts.n: 7.12.A.1 (topic 7.12), skill 5.F. Thinking: rebuild the Ksp expression with a common ion already present and keep the 2 : 1 ratio of X⁻ to dissolved MX₂. Trap: (A), [X⁻] = s.

parts.q:
To demonstrate the common-ion effect, the student plans to repeat the whole procedure using 0.050 M NaX(aq) in place of distilled water in step 1, and to show that the residue in step 4 has less mass than 0.0500 g. Which of the following best evaluates the plan?
(A) It is valid: a residue lighter than 0.0500 g would show that the added X⁻ lowers the solubility of MX₂.
(B) It is flawed: the common-ion effect raises the solubility of MX₂, so the residue should be heavier, not lighter.
(C) It is flawed: the residue would also contain the dissolved NaX, so its mass would not measure the MX₂ dissolved.
(D) It is flawed: MX₂ cannot dissolve at all in a solution that already contains X⁻, so there will be no residue.
parts.a: (C). Evaporating 100.0 mL of 0.050 M NaX leaves 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol of NaX in the dish, at least 0.2 g for any X, while the MX₂ that dissolves (about 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M, or 3 × 10⁻⁴ g) is a tiny fraction of that. The residue would be heavier than 0.0500 g and would say nothing about MX₂; the student needs a method that measures M²⁺ alone. (A) accepts a prediction the procedure cannot test. (B) has the common-ion effect backwards: adding X⁻ makes Q > Ksp for MX₂, so less of it dissolves. (D) overstates the effect: Q is below Ksp until [M²⁺] reaches Ksp/[X⁻]², so some MX₂ still dissolves.
parts.n: 7.12.A.1 (topic 7.12), skill 2.F. Thinking: judge whether a procedure's measurement still isolates the quantity of interest after a change to the procedure. Trap: (A), the right chemistry measured the wrong way.

mc.stem:
Questions 21-23 refer to the following.

Methanol is made from carbon monoxide and hydrogen:
CO(g) + 2 H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g)   (the forward reaction is exothermic)
A graph shows the partial pressures of the three gases in a sealed vessel against time. The system starts at equilibrium at temperature T with P(CO) = 1.00 atm, P(H₂) = 2.00 atm and P(CH₃OH) = 0.40 atm. One change is made at each of the times t₁, t₂ and t₃, and the system reaches a new equilibrium before the next change. The graph shows the following.
At t₁: P(H₂) jumps to 3.00 atm while the other two stay the same; then P(H₂) and P(CO) fall gradually and P(CH₃OH) rises gradually, leveling off at P(CO) = 0.82 atm, P(H₂) = 2.65 atm and P(CH₃OH) = 0.58 atm.
At t₂: all three partial pressures jump at the same instant to twice their values (1.64, 5.30 and 1.16 atm); then P(CO) and P(H₂) fall gradually and P(CH₃OH) rises gradually, leveling off at 1.04, 4.11 and 1.76 atm.
At t₃: none of the partial pressures jumps; P(CO) and P(H₂) rise gradually and P(CH₃OH) falls gradually, leveling off at 1.33, 4.69 and 1.47 atm.

parts.q:
Which change was made at t₃?
(A) The temperature of the vessel was raised.
(B) A catalyst was added to the vessel.
(C) Some CH₃OH was removed from the vessel.
(D) The volume of the vessel was increased.
parts.a: (A). No partial pressure jumps at t₃, so the change did not alter Q; the system nevertheless moved to a new position, so K must have changed, and only temperature changes K. The shift is toward CO and H₂, so K decreased, and for an exothermic forward reaction K decreases when the temperature rises. (B) A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally and does not move an equilibrium at all. (C) Removing CH₃OH would show as a sudden drop in P(CH₃OH), followed by a shift that makes more CH₃OH and uses up CO and H₂, the opposite of what is seen. (D) A larger volume would make all three partial pressures drop suddenly at t₃.
parts.n: 7.10.A.2 and 7.9.A.1 (topic 7.10), skill 5.D. Thinking: a gradual shift with no jump means K changed rather than Q. Trap: (B), a catalyst, because 'the graph changed without anything being added or removed'.

parts.q:
Immediately after the change at t₂, how does Qp compare with Kp, and what happens next?
(A) Qp = 4Kp, so the net reaction proceeds toward CO and H₂.
(B) Qp = Kp/4, so the net reaction proceeds toward CH₃OH.
(C) Qp = Kp/2, so the net reaction proceeds toward CH₃OH.
(D) Qp = Kp, so no net reaction occurs after the change.
parts.a: (B). Just before t₂ the system is at equilibrium, Qp = P(CH₃OH)/[P(CO)P(H₂)²] = Kp. Doubling every partial pressure multiplies the numerator by 2 and the denominator by 2 × 2² = 8, so Qp = 2/8 × Kp = Kp/4 (numerically 1.16 ÷ (1.64 × 5.30²) = 0.025, against Kp = 0.10). Qp < Kp, so the net reaction makes CH₃OH, as the graph shows. (A) inverts the effect of the doubling. (C) forgets to square P(H₂), giving 2/(2 × 2) = ½. (D) confuses Qp with Kp: the compression leaves Kp unchanged but changes Qp.
parts.n: 7.10.A.1 (topic 7.10), skill 5.F. Thinking: turn a sudden change in pressure into a factor on Q, using the exponents. Trap: (C), leaving out the square on P(H₂).

parts.q:
A student notes that P(CO) at the equilibrium reached after t₂ (1.04 atm) is higher than at the equilibrium just before t₂ (0.82 atm). She concludes that the change at t₂ shifted the equilibrium toward CO and H₂. Which of the following best evaluates her conclusion?
(A) It is correct: a higher equilibrium pressure of a reactant can only come from a shift toward the reactants.
(B) It is correct: compressing a gas mixture favors the side of the equation that has more moles of gas.
(C) It is incorrect: the change at t₂ also changed Kp, so the two equilibrium states cannot be compared.
(D) It is incorrect: the compression doubled P(CO) to 1.64 atm, and the net reaction then lowered it to 1.04 atm.
parts.a: (D). At t₂ the vessel was compressed to half its volume, which doubled every partial pressure at once. The system then responded by net forward reaction: P(CO) fell from 1.64 to 1.04 atm while P(CH₃OH) rose from 1.16 to 1.76 atm. The shift was toward CH₃OH; it only partly offset the compression, which is why P(CO) ends above 0.82 atm. (A) compares two equilibrium states and ignores the sudden jump between them. (B) has Le Chatelier's rule backwards: compression favors the side with fewer moles of gas, here CH₃OH. (C) is wrong because a volume change at constant temperature leaves Kp unchanged.
parts.n: 7.9.A.1 and 7.10.A.1 (topic 7.9), skill 6.B. Thinking: separate the sudden effect of a stress from the system's gradual response to it. Trap: (A), comparing only the two plateaus.

parts.q:
A rigid 1.00 L flask holds an equilibrium mixture of 0.0300 mol NO₂ and 0.0200 mol N₂O₄ at constant temperature: 2 NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). All of its nitrogen is ¹⁴N. A student injects a trace of ¹⁵NO₂, too little to change either amount. An analysis then shows that 57% of the ¹⁵N atoms are in N₂O₄ molecules and 43% are in NO₂ molecules, and the split is the same an hour later. Which conclusion do these results best support?
(A) The ¹⁵N favors N₂O₄: an even spread would put only 40% of it there, the fraction of the molecules that are N₂O₄.
(B) The ¹⁵N has not finished spreading, since an even spread would put equal amounts of it in NO₂ and in N₂O₄.
(C) The ¹⁵N is spread in proportion to the nitrogen atoms in each species, so NO₂ and N₂O₄ kept interconverting.
(D) The ¹⁵N entered N₂O₄ only while the injected gas mixed in; after that, the two species stopped interconverting.
parts.a: (C). The flask holds 0.0300 mol of N atoms in NO₂ and 2 × 0.0200 = 0.0400 mol in N₂O₄, so if every nitrogen atom is equally likely to carry the label, 0.0400 ÷ 0.0700 = 57% of the ¹⁵N is in N₂O₄ and 43% in NO₂, which is what was measured. The label went in as NO₂, and the trace was too small to change either amount, so no net reaction was needed; ¹⁵N reached N₂O₄ only because NO₂ molecules kept combining while an equal number of N₂O₄ molecules split apart. That is dynamic equilibrium. (A) counts molecules instead of atoms: 0.0200 ÷ 0.0500 = 40% of the molecules are N₂O₄, but each carries two N atoms. (B) takes an even spread to mean equal shares for the two species, and a split that is unchanged an hour later has finished spreading. (D) describes a static equilibrium: the injection did not disturb the equilibrium, so there was no net reaction to carry the label into N₂O₄, and a split that matches the atom proportions exactly is what continued exchange produces.
parts.n: 7.1.A.1 and 7.1.A.3 (topic 7.1), skill 6.B. Thinking: work out where a tracer ends up if the forward and reverse reactions keep running, and compare with the measured split. Trap: (A), counting molecules instead of nitrogen atoms.

parts.q:
Barium sulfate is swallowed as a suspension before some X-ray images are taken; the solid is harmless, but dissolved Ba²⁺ is toxic. A chemist designing a suspension considers adding enough Na₂SO₄ to make the liquid 0.10 M in sulfate. For BaSO₄, Ksp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. Compared with a saturated solution of BaSO₄ in pure water, what would [Ba²⁺] be in the 0.10 M sulfate solution at 25 °C?
(A) 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ M, about 2 × 10⁴ times lower
(B) 1.1 × 10⁻⁹ M, about 1 × 10⁴ times lower
(C) 1.1 × 10⁻¹¹ M, about 1 × 10⁶ times lower
(D) 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, the same as in pure water
parts.a: (B). In pure water, [Ba²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M. With [SO₄²⁻] fixed at 0.10 M by the Na₂SO₄, [Ba²⁺] = Ksp/[SO₄²⁻] = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 0.10 = 1.1 × 10⁻⁹ M, lower by a factor of about 9.5 × 10³, roughly 10⁴. (A) doubles the sulfate concentration, confusing the two Na⁺ per formula unit with two sulfate ions. (C) multiplies Ksp by 0.10 instead of dividing. (D) treats a constant Ksp as a constant solubility, ignoring the common ion.
parts.n: 7.12.A.1 and 7.11.A.2 (topic 7.12), skill 5.F. Thinking: apply the common-ion effect quantitatively in an unfamiliar medical setting. Trap: (A), the 2 in Na₂SO₄ applied to sulfate.

fr.title: Ammonium carbamate: an equilibrium measured by pressure
fr.stem:
Solid ammonium carbamate, NH₂COONH₄ (molar mass 78.07 g/mol), decomposes reversibly when warmed:
NH₂COONH₄(s) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g) + CO₂(g)
A student places a sample of the solid in the same evacuated, rigid flask in each trial, holds the flask at a constant temperature, and records the total gas pressure once it stops changing. The only gases in the flask come from the decomposition.
Trial · temperature · mass of solid added (g) · final total pressure (atm) · solid left at the end?
1 · T₁ · 1.00 · 0.240 · yes
2 · T₁ · 2.00 · 0.240 · yes
3 · T₂ · 1.00 · 0.420 · yes
4 · T₁ · 0.078 · 0.150 · no
Temperature T₂ is higher than T₁.

parts.q: Calculate the value of Kp at T₁, using the results of trial 1.
parts.a: Kp = 2.05 × 10⁻³. The gases form in a 2 : 1 mole ratio, so P(NH₃) = ⅔ × 0.240 = 0.160 atm and P(CO₂) = ⅓ × 0.240 = 0.080 atm (1 point). The solid does not appear in the expression, so Kp = P(NH₃)²·P(CO₂) = (0.160)²(0.080) = 2.05 × 10⁻³ (1 point).
parts.n: Using 0.240 atm for each gas, splitting the pressure equally (0.120 atm each), or leaving out the square on P(NH₃) earns no second point. An expression with the solid in the denominator earns nothing.

parts.q: Trials 1 and 2 used different masses of solid but gave the same final pressure. Explain why, in terms of the equilibrium expression.
