parts.a: The solid is not in the Kp expression, so as long as some solid is present the equilibrium requires P(NH₃)²·P(CO₂) = Kp, with the gases in the fixed 2 : 1 ratio. At a given temperature only one total pressure (0.240 atm at T₁) satisfies this, whatever the mass of solid.
parts.n: 'The flask was full' or 'the extra solid did not react' earns nothing: the point is that the amount of solid does not enter Q or K.

parts.q: A student claims that trial 4 shows that the value of Kp depends on the amount of solid used. Evaluate the claim, using a calculation of Qp for the gas in trial 4.
parts.a: The claim is wrong. In trial 4, P(NH₃) = ⅔ × 0.150 = 0.100 atm and P(CO₂) = 0.0500 atm, so Qp = (0.100)²(0.0500) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, which is less than Kp = 2.05 × 10⁻³ (1 point). The 0.078 g (0.0010 mol) of solid decomposed completely before Qp could reach Kp. With no solid left there is no equilibrium, so trial 4 says nothing about Kp, which depends only on temperature (1 point).
parts.n: Agreeing with the claim earns nothing. 'Kp is a constant' with no Qp calculation and no mention that the solid ran out earns at most the second point.

parts.q: Use trial 3 to determine whether the decomposition is endothermic or exothermic. Justify your answer.
parts.a: Endothermic. At T₂, P(NH₃) = 0.280 atm and P(CO₂) = 0.140 atm, so Kp = (0.280)²(0.140) = 1.10 × 10⁻², larger than 2.05 × 10⁻³ at T₁. K increases as the temperature rises only when the forward reaction absorbs heat.
parts.n: 'Endothermic, because the pressure went up' with no link to K, or with the reason 'heating speeds up the reaction', earns nothing.

parts.q: The flask from trial 1, at equilibrium at T₁ with solid present, is injected with extra NH₃(g) until P(NH₃) is momentarily 0.320 atm. (i) Predict whether the mass of solid in the flask increases, decreases or stays the same as a new equilibrium is established. (ii) Determine whether P(CO₂) at the new equilibrium is greater than, less than or equal to 0.080 atm. Justify both answers.
parts.a: (i) The mass of solid increases. Right after the injection Qp = (0.320)²(0.080) = 8.19 × 10⁻³, four times Kp, so there is net reverse reaction: NH₃ and CO₂ combine to form solid NH₂COONH₄ (1 point). (ii) Less than 0.080 atm. The reverse reaction consumes CO₂. Also, at the new equilibrium P(NH₃) is still above 0.160 atm (the reverse reaction removes only part of the added NH₃), so P(CO₂) = Kp / P(NH₃)² must be below 0.080 atm (1 point). (Solving gives P(NH₃) = 0.234 atm and P(CO₂) = 0.037 atm.)
parts.n: 'The solid is not in K, so adding NH₃ does not change its mass' earns nothing for (i). 'P(CO₂) returns to 0.080 atm because K is unchanged' earns nothing for (ii): K is unchanged, but P(NH₃) is not.

parts.q: In another run at T₁, the flask was not fully evacuated and held 0.020 atm of air before the solid was added. The student treated the measured total pressure as P(NH₃) + P(CO₂). Would the calculated Kp be too high, too low or unaffected? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Too high. The air does not take part in the reaction, so the equilibrium pressures of NH₃ and CO₂ are unchanged, but the gauge would read 0.260 atm. Dividing 0.260 atm in a 2 : 1 ratio overstates both partial pressures and gives Kp = (0.173)²(0.0867) = 2.60 × 10⁻³ instead of 2.05 × 10⁻³.
parts.n: 'Unaffected, because air is not in the Kp expression' earns nothing: air is not in Kp, but it is in the student's measurement. 'Too low' earns nothing.

parts.q: Describe an experiment, using the same flask at T₁, that would show that 0.240 atm is an equilibrium pressure and not simply the pressure at which the solid stopped decomposing.
parts.a: Approach equilibrium from the other side. Put some solid NH₂COONH₄ in the flask, then add NH₃ and CO₂ in a 2 : 1 ratio to a total pressure above 0.240 atm (for example 0.40 atm) and hold the flask at T₁. If the pressure falls, as solid forms, and levels off at 0.240 atm, the same state is reached from both directions, which is the mark of an equilibrium.
parts.n: 'Wait longer' or 'repeat trial 1' earns nothing: both approach the state from the same direction. Adding the gases without any solid, or in a ratio other than 2 : 1, earns nothing, since the final pressure would then not be expected to be 0.240 atm.

fr.title: Esterification: measuring K by titration
fr.stem:
Ethanoic acid (acetic acid) and ethanol react to form ethyl ethanoate and water. All four substances are liquids that mix completely with one another:
CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l)
A student mixes 0.500 mol CH₃COOH and 0.500 mol C₂H₅OH with a strong-acid catalyst that supplies 0.0100 mol of H⁺ and a negligible amount of water. She seals the flask and leaves it at room temperature for a week, until the composition stops changing. She then titrates all the acid in the flask, the ethanoic acid and the catalyst together, with 1.00 M NaOH(aq). The endpoint is reached after 176.7 mL of NaOH(aq) is added.

parts.q: Calculate the value of the equilibrium constant, K, for the reaction.
parts.a: K = 4.0. The NaOH neutralizes 0.1767 L × 1.00 M = 0.1767 mol of acid, of which 0.0100 mol is the catalyst, so 0.1667 mol CH₃COOH remains at equilibrium. Then 0.500 − 0.1667 = 0.3333 mol of acid reacted, forming 0.3333 mol of ester and 0.3333 mol of water and leaving 0.1667 mol of ethanol (1 point). The volume V cancels because each side has two terms: K = (0.3333/V)(0.3333/V) ÷ [(0.1667/V)(0.1667/V)] = 4.0 (1 point).
parts.n: Forgetting to subtract the catalyst earns no first point. Leaving water out of the expression, or inverting it (0.25), earns no second point.

parts.q: A classmate says that water should be left out of the equilibrium expression, because it is a liquid. Do you agree or disagree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Disagree. Liquids and solids are left out only when their concentration does not depend on how much is present, as for a pure liquid or a solvent in large excess. Here water is one component of a mixture, formed in amounts comparable to the other three, so its concentration changes as the reaction proceeds and must appear in K. (Leaving it out would also make K depend on the volume of the mixture.)
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'Disagree, because water is a product' with no reason why this water, unlike a solvent, has a changing concentration earns nothing.

parts.q: Another student used the same data but forgot to account for the catalyst in the titration. Would that student's value of K be too high, too low or unaffected? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Too low. Taking all 0.1767 mol of titrated acid as CH₃COOH overstates the unreacted acid, and so the unreacted ethanol, and understates the ester and water (0.3233 mol each). Larger reactant terms and smaller product terms give K = (0.3233)² ÷ (0.1767)² = 3.3, lower than 4.0.
parts.n: 'Too high, because more acid was titrated' earns nothing; so does a direction with no link to how the acid amount enters the expression.

fr.title: Bromine chloride: when the shortcut fails
fr.stem:
At a certain temperature, Kc = 0.25 for the equilibrium
2 BrCl(g) ⇌ Br₂(g) + Cl₂(g)
A 0.200 mol sample of pure BrCl(g) is placed in an evacuated, rigid 1.00 L flask at this temperature and allowed to reach equilibrium. Br₂ is a red-brown gas.

parts.q: Calculate [Br₂] at equilibrium.
parts.a: [Br₂] = 0.0500 M. If x mol/L of Br₂ forms, [Cl₂] = x and [BrCl] = 0.200 − 2x, so x²/(0.200 − 2x)² = 0.25. Taking the square root of both sides: x/(0.200 − 2x) = 0.50, so x = 0.100 − x and x = 0.0500 M (with [BrCl] = 0.100 M; check: (0.0500)² ÷ (0.100)² = 0.25).
parts.n: Using 0.200 − x for [BrCl] (answer 0.0667 M) earns nothing; so does any answer that leaves no BrCl.

parts.q: A classmate assumes that 0.200 − 2x ≈ 0.200, solves x²/(0.200)² = 0.25, and reports [Br₂] = 0.100 M. Explain why this answer cannot be correct, without solving the equilibrium again.
parts.a: If [Br₂] were 0.100 M, then 2 × 0.100 = 0.200 M of BrCl would have reacted, leaving [BrCl] = 0, which is impossible at equilibrium: some reactant must remain, and with [BrCl] = 0 the quotient would be undefined, not 0.25. The shortcut is valid only when 2x is small compared with 0.200 M, and a K as large as 0.25 gives no reason to expect that.
parts.n: 'The classmate made an algebra mistake' earns nothing: the algebra is right; the assumption is not. 'K is small, so the assumption is fine' earns nothing.

parts.q: The equilibrium mixture is compressed to 0.500 L at constant temperature. Predict whether the number of moles of Br₂ increases, decreases or stays the same. Justify your prediction by referring to Q.
parts.a: It stays the same. Halving the volume doubles every concentration, so Q = [Br₂][Cl₂]/[BrCl]² becomes (2 × 2)/2² = 1 times its old value: Q still equals K. With 2 mol of gas on each side, there is no net reaction, and the moles of every species are unchanged.
parts.n: 'It increases, because pressure favors the product side' earns nothing. 'It stays the same' with no reference to Q or to the equal numbers of moles of gas earns nothing.

parts.q: When the flask is compressed, the student sees the color of the gas mixture become darker. The student claims that the darker color shows that the compression shifted the equilibrium toward Br₂. Evaluate the claim.
parts.a: The claim is wrong. As shown in part (c), there is no shift. The color darkens because the same number of Br₂ molecules now occupies half the volume, so [Br₂] doubles, from 0.0500 M to 0.100 M, and the gas absorbs more light. A darker color shows a higher concentration, not a larger amount.
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'Disagree, because pressure does not affect equilibrium' with no mention of the doubled concentration earns nothing.
